text:
The spy who betrayed his country for 'Viagra' | The Independent

Ben Macintyre’s extraordinary new book tells the real story of a KGB officer who offered to betray the Soviet Union in the hope that Western medicine could save his marriage. The author tells Guy Walters how governments may devise codenames and clandestine networks, but spies are more often than not motivated by human vulnerability than doctrine

On a hot autumn evening in Tehran in 1981, two spies sat drinking vodka in a small white-tiled bathroom. One, Ian McCredie, was British; the other, Vladimir Kuzichkin, was a KGB major, more than six feet four inches tall and so broad that the wicker laundry basket beneath him creaked. The cold taps ran into the bath and basin, while a radio played to mask their voices from Iranian listening devices. If they were overheard, both men risked arrest, torture and perhaps execution.

The Russian had already offered to betray the KGB, and possessed a secret of potentially enormous value. It appeared that Soviet-backed communists were preparing for the possibility of seizing power in Iran and inviting in the Red Army, giving Moscow access to the country’s oilfields and the ports on the Persian Gulf. Kuzichkin revealed what he wanted in exchange; he believed Western medicine could cure something that was destroying his marriage – erectile dysfunction.

Ben Macintyre’s terrific new book, Redwood: The Untold Story of the Cold War’s Most Extraordinary Spy, begins here, with a scene that dismantles the idea that history is shaped only by grand strategy, ideology and powerful states.

“I was first told about it ten years ago, and I didn’t believe it,” Macintyre tells me. “I love this story. One man’s very private, very secret problem, and it can be a hinge of history.”

Kuzichkin’s vulnerability had roots far deeper than his unhappy sex life. Born in Moscow in 1947, he was raised as the son of Andrei Kuzichkin, a violent, alcoholic and embittered KGB officer. At 22, he discovered that Andrei was not his biological father. His real father was Georgi Larkin, a construction engineer of Irish ancestry who had died in Siberia before Vladimir could meet him. The revelation fractured his sense of identity, but also offered the possibility that he could become somebody else.

He joined the Communist Party and married Galina Kokosova, a diminutive, secretly religious young woman whom he adored. After university, he entered the KGB and was eventually posted to Iran, where revolution had swept away the Shah and replaced his regime with the Islamic Republic of Ayatollah Khomeini. The country became a crucible of violence, conspiracy and espionage, as Islamists, nationalists and Marxists fought to determine its future while Iran was also at war with Iraq.

Kuzichkin served under diplomatic cover as a vice-consul, but his real work included liaison with the Tudeh, Iran’s communist party. The Tudeh received Soviet money and direction, and had constructed a clandestine network extending into the armed forces. With the USSR already occupying neighbouring Afghanistan, Western governments feared that a communist coup in Tehran could bring Soviet forces to the Gulf and, in the worst scenario, set the superpowers on a path towards nuclear confrontation.

“From every point of view, this was a genuine threat. A real fear,” Macintyre says.

By the time he approached the British, Kuzichkin had become disgusted by Soviet corruption and the KGB’s manipulation of Iranian politics. But Macintyre does not turn him into a spotless ideological dissident. His motives were political, psychological and painfully physical.

He was drinking heavily, feared losing Galina and had developed an almost mystical belief that Western doctors possessed a pill denied to Soviet medicine. If MI6 could restore his potency, he imagined, it might restore his marriage too.

His first approach was appropriately confused. Kuzichkin walked into the British embassy and announced to the diplomat Nicholas Barrington: “I am KGB. I wish to defect to UK.” He had selected Barrington because the KGB mistakenly believed the flamboyant, impeccably dressed envoy must be MI6’s man in Tehran. But Barrington was not a spy at all. The offer was passed instead to McCredie, a young intelligence officer working under diplomatic cover, who had to decide whether this implausibly valuable Russian was genuine, a KGB “dangle”, or bait in an Iranian trap.

MI6 gave Kuzichkin the codename REDWOOD, inspired by his immense height. McCredie concealed him beneath a blanket in the back of a Land Rover to bring him into the British compound, where the bathroom became their improvised safe house. MI6 supplied pills – which were nothing more than vitamin tablets as this was a pre-viagra era – and an elderly Minox camera. Kuzichkin would then return exposed film in cigarette packets during fleeting “brush contacts”. Every encounter risked detection by the KGB or Iran’s competing security organisations.

“McCredie is an extraordinary figure,” Macintyre says. “You think you’re getting to know him, and then you’re not sure that you know him at all. Clearly this operation was the most important part of his life, and his relationship with Kuzichkin was the defining relationship of his life. The dangers he was under were absolutely terrifying – if he had been caught… The stakes were very high.”

That is partly because REDWOOD demonstrates a central truth of agent-running: spies are recruited through human needs, which seldom fit the tidy acronym of money, ideology, coercion and ego, often known as MICE. Kuzichkin wanted to challenge a system he had come to despise, but also to save his marriage to the woman he loved. His courage was inseparable from shame, loneliness and fear.

He began supplying information about KGB personnel, secret communications, Soviet operations and the Tudeh underground. The material was extraordinarily valuable, but it also posed an increasingly dark question: who would ultimately use it, and to what end? As the operation moves towards its most dangerous phase, Macintyre transforms a tale of brilliant tradecraft into a moral inquiry. To reveal the outcome would be a plot spoiler, but the legacy of the operation remains fiercely disputed.

“There is still some ambivalence about the story,” Macintyre says. “Some say that it was totally justified, the more gung-ho brigade. Others say that the butcher’s bill was too high. But you have to remember that this wasn’t MI6 acting rogue. It was ultimately a political decision.”

Interestingly, the service made no attempt to obstruct his research. “MI6’s attitude to secrecy is changing,” he says. “I think it’s much more realistic these days. But nobody wants to be the next Tomlinson” – a reference to former MI6 officer Richard Tomlinson, whose disclosures led to prosecution and years of legal conflict.

The remark points to one of Redwood’s most unsettling themes. Intelligence operations do not end when the secret has been obtained or a case officially closed. Information develops an afterlife, passing into other hands and colliding with calculations its source may never have anticipated. A tactical triumph can become a strategic disaster; the enemy of an enemy may prove still more dangerous.

That ambiguity makes a story from the 1980s feel disconcertingly current. The apparatus of espionage has been transformed by satellites, cyberwarfare and mass interception, yet Macintyre believes human intelligence – Humint – has become more valuable today rather than less.

“The reality is that espionage is more important than it has ever been,” he says. “There’s been this feeling that cyber will take over, and that espionage is now basically all about interception. But Humint is now more important than ever. Sigint is very easy to corrupt. We are going back to a more analogue way, a more old-fashioned way.”

Signals intelligence may capture what an organisation is saying, but a human source can reveal whether its leaders believe it, whether subordinates are merely supplying the answers demanded of them, or whether an entire intelligence apparatus is lying to itself. Macintyre sees Vladimir Putin’s assault on Ukraine as the supreme modern example.

“The biggest intelligence mistake was Putin invading Ukraine,” he says. “He was told by the FSB that he could almost walk in.”

Russia has also revived the “illegal”, an intelligence officer living under a false civilian identity without diplomatic cover. “There are spies among us, and there are illegals all over the place,” Macintyre says. “This is something straight out of the Cold War playbook. There are more illegals operating in the West than during the time of the Soviet Union.”

Like the best of Macintyre’s books, Redwood is less concerned with the machinery of espionage than with the unruly people caught inside it. States may devise codenames, doctrines and clandestine networks, but secrets are carried by vulnerable and messy human beings. The most sophisticated intelligence system can still turn upon love, vanity, terror or humiliation – and the course of history upon a whispered bargain in a Tehran bathroom.

Redwood is published 10 September. Ben Macintyre will be live on stage at the How To Academy on Tuesday 8 September, 7:30pm – 8:45pm, at the Emmanuel Centre, Marsham St, London, SW1P 3DW.

777 In praise of Zionism, the most successful national liberation movement of the modern age.

PIERRE REHOV WRITES: "That is the story worth telling, and it has been buried under seventy years of accumulated slander so thick that most educated Westerners now believe the exact inverse of every load-bearing fact.

* WHAT ZIONISM ACTUALY IS? Zionism is the national liberation movement of the Jewish people. That is the whole definition.

It holds that the Jews constitute a nation, that nations are entitled to self-determination in their ancestral homeland, and that the Jewish homeland is the strip of land between the Jordan and the Mediterranean - where Jewish peoplehood was formed, where Jewish law was written, where Jewish kings ruled, and toward which every Jew in every exile prayed three times a day for nineteen centuries without a single year’s interruption.

* ZIONISM-The word was coined by Nathan Birnbaum in 1890. The idea is considerably older than the word. It predates European colonialism by two thousand years, and it predates the modern nation-state by roughly the same margin.

Every other national movement of the twentieth century is granted this framing automatically. Their aspiration to a state of their own is treated as the natural expression of a people’s dignity. Only in the Jewish case is the identical aspiration reclassified as a crime...

The demand that Jews alone forgo, what everyone else is granted by default, has a name, and the name has not changed since the Middle Ages.

The nineteenth century offered the Jews of Europe a deal. Assimilate, stop being conspicuous, dress like your neighbours, speak their language, serve in their armies, and you will be accepted as citizens.

Millions of Jews took the deal in perfect good faith. They became German patriots, French officers, Austrian professors, Russian doctors. They gave Europe its physics and its music and its jurisprudence.

The deal was a fraud, and it was exposed twice within twenty years.

In Europe Six million people were murdered because there was no government on earth obliged to defend them, no army that would come, no embassy that would issue papers, no navy that would sail.

And then, in the decades after 1948, roughly 850,000 Jews were driven out of Baghdad, Cairo, Damascus, Aleppo, Tripoli, Sanaa, Fez and Algiers, communities that in some cases predated Islam by a thousand years, their property confiscated, their citizenship revoked, their synagogues burned.

They were absorbed by Israel, almost entirely bankrupt, new country of 800,000 people, - that took them in without conditions and without international funding, and today their descendants make up more than half the Jewish population of Israel. The world has never once been asked to consider them refugees.

Zionism was the correct answer to a question that Europe and the Arab world posed with unmistakable clarity. The Jews who understood it early lived. The ones who waited for civilization to protect them died.

* THE LAND THEY CAME TO: The Palestine of the nineteenth century was one of the most neglected backwaters of a decomposing empire. Every Western traveler, who crossed it in that century, recorded the same impression, and they were not coordinating. The land was not empty. It was exhausted, depopulated relative to any capacity it had ever had, and dying.

This is the territory that the first Zionist pioneers bought. Bought, at inflated prices, in cash, from willing sellers, with money raised from Jewish farmers and Jewish shopkeepers across Europe. The buyers drained it by hand. Many of them died of malaria doing it. That is the colonial conquest the world has been instructed to condemn.

Here is the fact that detonates the entire modern narrative, and it comes from British colonial records rather than from any Israeli source.

Between the census of 1922 and the end of the Mandate, the Arab population of Palestine grew at a rate that no natural increase in the region could explain.

https://t.co/CpJySCgQt8

According to Press Monitor's tracking of Indian publications, this press review delivers essential media intelligence on today's news on commercial shipping and ports. Our media monitoring of Indian print outlets captures seven developments that matter for maritime professionals, logistics operators, and energy markets.

1. Western Dedicated Freight Corridor Completion
A front-page report in Business Standard says Prime Minister Narendra Modi dedicated the Rs 73,000 crore Western Dedicated Freight Corridor to the nation on 8 September in New Delhi. The 2,800 km corridor connects Dadri in Uttar Pradesh with Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority and is expected to cut freight transit time by about 60 per cent. The project, first proposed by former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, links northern industrial centres with major ports including Mundra, Kandla, Pipavav and JNPA.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the final sections of the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor, completing the 1,506-kilometre route connecting Jawaharlal Nehru Port in Navi Mumbai with Dadri in Uttar Pradesh. Why it matters: The Rs 73,000 crore project cuts freight transit time by 60 per cent and positions India's logistics sector for global competitiveness. Key detail: The corridor spans six states and enables double-stack container trains to haul cargo equivalent to over 250 trucks per journey. Source: Business Standard. Next step: Monitor freight rate impacts on maritime port throughput. How will this reshape India's export competitiveness?

2. Houthi Strikes on Saudi Energy Facilities
A front-page report in Business Line says Saudi Arabia halted several key energy facilities after Iran-backed Houthi militants claimed fresh missile and drone strikes on sites near the Yemen border. The attacks, which targeted Aramco infrastructure in Abha, Najran and Jazan, have ignited fires and injured over seventy individuals while raising fears of prolonged supply disruptions that are pushing Brent crude prices toward one hundred dollars a barrel. Market analysts warn that ongoing hostilities, compounded by heightened Iran-United States tensions and restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz, could sustain shipping blockades well into twenty twenty seven.

5. Wheat, Maize and Rice Prices Steady

text:
【 jamaican blue mountain. 

he could vaguely recall sojiro's voice back from when he was a teenager. 

not all bags that say "blue mountain" are actually the real variety, so it takes a bit of care to source these sometimes. avoid labels with the words "style" or "blend" as it may be —

the nostalgia is comforting after all this time. 

it's a full body with a mild flavor, naturally creamy, a hint of chocolate and no bitterness. something of a small game of his, when goro handles breakfast, akira finds the most suitable coffee blend to match. 

guatemalan antiqua for eggs and bacon days. sumatra or mexican altura for rice porridge, when akira wakes up with another migrane and asks for something mild that won't make him throw up his painkillers. 

...

akira takes a long sip of his own cup, and it compliments the chocolate in the crepes somehow perfectly. 

he tries not to make it too obvious, but there's a subtle glance made towards goro, almost as if he's waiting for the man to take his first sip. 

and his traitorous heart flutters without his consent when he does. 

he wants to think he's looking at him for traces of that relationship exhaustion he implied earlier, but it's hard to tell from general exhaustion. it blurs together with those habits of his, to look at his expression and how it subtly changes. 

when he's genuinely happy, his eyes don't express that. his smiles feel reversed somehow, and yet never really not suit him. 

he wonders what those eyes or that smile will resemble when he finally admits that akira's become unbearable, forced his love or his affections onto goro for long enough, and that he — 】

...hm? 

【 there's a takeout tray, goro's tray, and the man is motioning towards his food with a half blur of words that akira forgot to fully comprehend. 】

try? 

【 the red of the berries looked very fresh somehow, and he quietly held his fork over, pressed down into a spot at the end, and scooped up a bite of his. 

... strawberries and cream. 

his eyes shut as he chews. the crepes from this store are perfectly cooked, light and airy, and not too sweet. it doesn't take more than a moment before he's done, and he supposes he could offer some of his own. 

it's not even a thought in that head of his, he could push his meal over too, but he finds himself just getting a little off his own, and quietly offering goro the bite from his own fork. 

the sort of idiotic sentiments he'd pull on some of their lighter days and not one which they were stuck in place. 

but he doesn't know how to stop. 

he's forgotten how to be casual a long time ago. 】

text:
THE TRANSPARENCY TEST: WHO IS ACTUALLY TRYING TO KEEP THE RECORD FROM THE PUBLIC?

Eculaw Group. Law. Rights. Accountability. Part 4 of a 5-part series.
By Eculaw Editorial Team

If there is one place where Atiku and Tinubu FBI records genuinely diverge, not in 2005 or 1993, but right now, in 2026, it is on the question of who is fighting to keep a U.S. government file closed.

THE FOIA FIGHT NOW UNDERWAY

Since 2022, transparency activist Aaron Greenspan has pursued FOIA requests against the FBI, DEA, IRS, State Department, and CIA for records relating to the 1990s Chicago heroin-trafficking investigation connected to Tinubu's forfeiture. That litigation, Greenspan v. FBI, et al., Civil Action No. 23-1816, is before Judge Beryl Howell in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. In April 2025, Judge Howell ruled that the FBI and DEA had improperly refused even to confirm or deny holding such records, and ordered them to process what they had. Tinubu did not stay out of that fight. He intervened, personally, as a party, and his lawyers have since filed briefs invoking FOIA Exemption 7(C) and the Privacy Act to argue that large portions of his own FBI and DEA file should stay redacted or withheld. In August 2026, Tinubu joined the Justice Department in seeking more time before responding to the court's disclosure order. That is a sitting head of state, through his own attorneys, actively litigating in an American court to narrow what the public gets to see of his own federal investigative file.

ATIKU'S DIFFERENT POSTURE

Atiku Abubakar is not a party to any comparable proceeding. There is no U.S. case in which he is asking a court to seal, redact, or withhold anything concerning himself. Whatever one makes of the 2005 search or the 2010 Senate report discussed in Part 3, both are sitting in the open historical record, discoverable by any reporter, without Atiku's lawyers standing in a Washington courtroom trying to keep the door closed. The Presidency's spokesman is correct that a U.S. judge, not Atiku, will decide the outcome of the FOIA case, but that observation does not touch the more basic point: Tinubu's side is the one asking for less to be released, not more.

A FIRSTHAND NOTE, FROM ECULAW'S FOUNDER

Eculaw's founder, Emeka Ugwuonye, Esq., served as counsel to the Nigerian Embassy in Washington in 2005 and offers the following firsthand account. In July of that year, he was asked by the Ambassador, on instruction understood to originate from President Olusegun Obasanjo, to prepare a legal opinion addressing whether Atiku, then still in the country, could be arrested by U.S. authorities before he departed. Obasanjo and Atiku were, by that point, in open political conflict, and an American legal cloud over his deputy would have served Obasanjo's interest in blocking Atiku's path to succeed him in 2007. He wrote an opinion stating the obvious and unremarkable legal truth: that the United States had the power to arrest anyone within its jurisdiction, but that he had no information indicating it intended to arrest Atiku. The Ambassador was visibly unsatisfied; he had wanted a categorical prediction of arrest, not a measured legal opinion. As he understands it, the FBI's search of the Potomac house did not occur until after Atiku had left U.S. soil, which is consistent with a search conducted as a matter of investigative process, not a manhunt aimed at a fleeing suspect. This account is offered as what it is: a personal recollection of a participant in the events of that period, not a court record. Readers may weigh it accordingly, alongside the documentary record set out in Parts 2 and 3 of this series.

THE PATTERN, ACROSS TWO DECADES

The pattern across two decades is consistent: Atiku's legal history is fully exposed and has been for twenty years, without him lifting a finger to shield it. Tinubu's legal history is, at this writing, the subject of an active, lawyered fight to keep parts of it sealed

text:
7 Pivotal Geopolitics Stories for Indian Decision Makers
https://t.co/muiZnXm9Ex

This press review draws on print media monitoring across Indian publications to track 7 major geopolitical developments. According to Press Monitor's tracking of Indian publications, these stories on news on geopolitics shape the landscape that Indian businesses and policymakers must navigate, powered by media monitoring and media intelligence.

1. Modi-Putin BRICS Bilateral Talks
A front-page report in Hindustan Times says Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi to discuss economic ties, energy cooperation including hydrocarbons and nuclear power, and global issues including the West Asia crisis and the Ukraine war. The summit, expected to see around twelve heads of state, will also see a sharp room crunch and tariff surge at luxury hotels in Delhi, with authorities working on a multi-airport plan to handle unprecedented air traffic from special aircraft and VIP delegations.
Why it matters: The most-covered story across 11 Indian newspapers, this meeting will shape India-Russia relations on the global stage.
Key detail: Hindustan Times reports the summit will see around twelve heads of state, with authorities working on a multi-airport plan to handle unprecedented air traffic from VIP delegations.
Source: Hindustan Times, New Delhi
Next step: Watch for defence and energy deals announced during the bilateral.

2. Trump-Putin Phone Call on Ukraine
A front-page report in Business Standard says US President Donald Trump told Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday that he wanted a swift end to the war in Ukraine, something that would allow US-Russia ties to be fully restored, the Kremlin said. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters that the pair had discussed the outcome of a weekend visit to Moscow and Kyiv by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and that Putin had told Trump what he believed the United States could do to help end the conflict. Both leaders rated the envoys' visit with a plus sign, agreed on the need to continue prisoner exchanges, and described the conversation as constructive while deciding to stay in touch by phone again if the need arose.
Why it matters: Covered by 5 major Indian dailies, the Trump-Putin call signals a potential shift in US-Russia relations with implications for global trade.
Key detail: Both leaders rated the envoys' visit with a plus sign and agreed on the need to continue prisoner exchanges, with Ukrainian President Zelenskyy noting three-way peace talks could occur as early as August.
Source: Business Standard, New Delhi
Next step: Monitor how India positions itself between the US and Russia on Ukraine.

3. India-China LAC Flag Meetings
A front-page report in Tribune says senior Indian and Chinese military commanders held two flag meetings over two days along the Line of Actual Control in Arunachal Pradesh. The first encounter occurred on Sunday between Corps Commander level officers at Wacha north of Kibithoo, followed by a second meeting on Monday at Damai on the Chinese side. Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed the interactions during a New Delhi briefing on Tuesday.
Why it matters: Three Indian papers reported on the first-ever Corps Commander-level flag meetings along the Line of Actual Control, signaling a thaw in military diplomacy.
Key detail: The meetings took place at Wacha on the Indian side and Damai on the Chinese side, with Lt Gen Girish Kalia leading the Indian delegation, ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping's expected visit for the BRICS summit.
Source: Tribune, New Delhi
Next step: Track whether these engagements lead to formal de-escalation protocols.

4. India Raises UN Map Border Row
A front-page report in Deccan Chronicle says Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold bilateral talks on Friday on the margins of the BRICS summit. The focus will be on deepening cooperation in areas of trade, investment, energy and technology.
Why it matters: Two major newspapers reported India's diplomatic pushback against a UN map inaccurately depicting Arunachal Pradesh and Aksai Chin as part of China.
Key detail: MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed at a biweekly briefing that the UN does not issue or endorse any maps, though some exist for consultation purposes, and India highlighted that a resolution on equal-area world maps does not constitute endorsement of national boundaries.
Source: Deccan Chronicle, New Delhi
Next step: Observe whether the UN takes corrective action on its cartographic materials.

5. Trump Map Sparks Diplomatic Outrage
A front-page report in Asian Age says President Donald Trump sparked international fury by posting a digital map colouring Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico and the Caribbean as United States territory. Iceland summoned the United States ambassador to denounce the image as wholly inappropriate amid escalating trade tensions and retaliatory tariffs between Washington and Ottawa. Separately, the Trump administration petitioned the Supreme Court to reinstate a federal immigration database for verifying state voter rolls following a lower court block.
Why it matters: Asian Age reports on Trump's controversial digital map colouring Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico and the Caribbean as US territory, sparking international fury.
Key detail: Iceland summoned the United States ambassador to denounce the image, amid escalating trade tensions and retaliatory tariffs between Washington and Ottawa, while the Trump administration also petitioned the Supreme Court to reinstate a federal immigration database.
Source: Asian Age, Washington
Next step: The diplomatic fallout could affect trade negotiations and multilateral cooperation.

6. India Seeks End to Ukraine War
A front-page report in Tribune says Modi met Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek on August 31 and urged moving from an endless war towards an end to the war. Peskov told Indian journalists in a virtual interaction ahead of Putin's visit to India for the BRICS summit. text:
The runway wasn't the biggest risk. What followed it was.

In 1968, construction began on an airport in the Big Cypress swamp that was meant to change South Florida's future.

Not a small airport. Six runways. A 39-square-mile site. A proposed 1,000-foot-wide transportation corridor carrying a highway and a high-speed monorail between Florida's coasts.

The National Park Service's history says the planned Everglades Jetport would have been five times the size of New York's JFK airport. The site lay just six miles north of Everglades National Park.

You can understand the pitch without agreeing with the location.

South Florida was growing. Aviation promised faster connections. Supersonic travel looked like the future, but aircraft breaking the sound barrier over populated neighborhoods posed an obvious problem. A remote site offered room and distance from those neighborhoods.

For people thinking about jobs, tourism, transportation and land values, this was not simply a runway. It was an economic engine waiting to start.

That was also the problem.

The common way to judge a project is to draw a boundary around it. How much land does it occupy? What happens inside the fence? Can the immediate damage be reduced?

But the boundary on the application is not necessarily the boundary of the consequences.

Russell Train, then an Interior Department undersecretary, asked hydrologist Luna Leopold to investigate. Leopold worked with scientist and conservationist Arthur Marshall and the National Park Service's Manuel Morris on an environmental impact report released in 1969.

Its warning went well beyond planes.

The report argued that the airport and its supporting facilities would trigger drainage and development for transportation, agriculture and services in Big Cypress, with destructive consequences for the wider South Florida ecosystem and Everglades National Park.

In other words: the project was not just what officials were building. It was what the project would make other people want to build next.

The same hotels, roads and businesses that made the airport attractive to its supporters made its location dangerous to its opponents.

A coalition of hunters, conservationists and citizen activists pushed back. Marjory Stoneman Douglas and the newly formed Friends of the Everglades were among those pressing for a different location.

In 1970, the Everglades Jetport Pact halted the work. The port authority began looking for another site. The six-runway vision left behind a single runway.

That outcome is easy to celebrate with hindsight. The decision itself raises a harder question.

How much future growth should a community count when it approves the first piece of infrastructure?

The strongest development argument is not that nature has no value. It is that a growing region needs places to put essential infrastructure. Moving noise away from homes solves a real problem. Transportation access can support livelihoods. Refusing one location does not eliminate the demand.

The strongest conservation argument is not that growth must stop. It is that some locations create costs that cannot be contained by the project's property lines. If a public investment opens sensitive land to a wave of development, reviewing only the first construction footprint misses the actual decision.

Both arguments deserve more than a slogan.

My perspective as a Miami real estate advisor: a promised road, station or airport is not automatically a reason to pay more for nearby property. First ask what has actually been approved, what remains contested and what additional development the infrastructure would enable.

Then ask the uncomfortable question: does the value depend on an assumption the community has not agreed to?

Buyers should be careful here. A compelling growth story can be real without being certain. A transportation proposal is not an entitlement. A construction start is not proof that the full plan will happen. And an improvement that benefits one parcel can impose costs far beyond it.

This is a historical lesson from the 1968-1970 jetport fight, not a claim about the site's current use or a prediction about today's projects.

The point is not to oppose every big idea. It is to evaluate the second and third moves before paying for the first.

Sometimes the most important line in a development plan is the one nobody has drawn yet.

Should infrastructure approvals account for the development they are likely to attract, or should each later project get its own separate review?

text:
Inspector General Promises 'Handcuffs Await' for Massive Corporate Visa Fraud for Foreign Labor | Teri Christoph, RedState

The U.S. Department of Labor is celebrating Labor Day by dropping the hammer on two major IT/data management companies, Cognizant and Cloudera, over alleged abuse of the H-1 B visa system.

In a tersely worded communication on X, Labor's Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito announced:

An hour later, D'Esposito was back on X.

One more.

@cloudera: PERM filings SUSPENDED.

@Sonderling47 @DOLOIG @WHFraudTF🇺🇸

At issue is the abuse of the Department of Labor's Program Electronic Review Management, aka PERM. This program permits employment-based permanent residency in the EB-2 and EB-3 categories. To qualify, the sponsoring employer must show two things: 1) There are not enough able, willing, qualified, and available U.S. workers (citizens, nationals, and lawful permanent residents) for the specific job in the intended area of employment and 2) hiring the foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages or working conditions of similarly employed U.S. workers.

Unfortunately, the system is rife with abuse and relies largely on the company's personal attestation. Jobs are sometimes listed in obscure publications widely distributed in (cough) certain countries that make up the majority of visa applicants in those categories, so the employer can say, truthfully as far as it goes, that no American applied. Sometimes companies portray themselves as the employer when, in reality, they serve as a body shop, subcontracting the immigrant labor to other companies and paying the worker a small fraction of the price they charge the workplace.

Busting Cognizant was particularly sweet.

This is the history. On June 9, 2026, Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds’ administration announced a managed-services deal with Cognizant and a cloud migration to Amazon Web Services, projecting more than $525 million in savings over 10 years. A later records release put combined payments at about $419.7 million over a decade, compared with an estimated $1.98 billion to keep the work in-house. A WARN notice listed roughly 192–200 state IT jobs ending August 3, 2026. Cognizant was to offer those workers jobs. Reynolds said IT operations were not a core state function and that modernization required private partners. This is a Republican governor.

When the crap hit the fan, Reynolds claimed that “at no point during our negotiations was it even considered to employ H-1B visa holders” and that the state and vendor were “fully committed from the onset to employing an Iowa-based workforce.” Unfortunately for Reynolds, when the contract terms became public, they clearly showed that offshore Indian workers were part of the deal.

Also of note, Iowa signed this contract two years after Cognizant was found guilty of employment discrimination by hiring Indian workers rather than Americans, and it had to pay a multi-million dollar settlement and fine. Ordinarily, that kind of track record would have warned off any potential governmental client. But it didn't.

This announcement, while welcome, was not a complete surprise. Back in July, D'Esposito announced DOL was undertaking a wide-ranging investigation into fraudulent visas, and Cognizant was in the crosshairs; see Labor Dept. IG Launches Probe on Criminals' Big Business Through H-1B Program – RedState.

Labour Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said officials have already issued multiple subpoenas as part of the large-scale probe into suspected labour trafficking and abuse of foreign worker programmes.

H-1B visa refers to a non-immigrant work permit that US employers use to hire professionals specialising in some occupations. Every year, thousands of Indians are hired using this visa.

"Without a doubt... we are going to take an aggressive action, which we believe is probably the most aggressive action against foreign labour fraud by an Inspector General, this administration," the senior official told Fox News in an interview. "We've already started to issue dozens of subpoenas."

He vowed to "track down every lead", and said whistleblowers had raised concerns over "some of the biggest companies, like Cognizant."

The investigators will "work side by side with the president and vice president's fraud task force" during the course of the probe, D'Esposito said.

Cloudera was already operating under a visa-fraud cloud. Back in April, Cloudera was hit with a lawsuit by the Department of Justice alleging it engaged in citizenship-status discrimination in PERM hiring from at least March 31, 2024, through January 28, 2025. Shortly thereafter, Labor's Employment and Training Administration announced it had suspended all PERM applications by or on behalf of Cloudera.

If one judges from the volume of filings and other public information, the Cloudera case is markedly different from that against Cognizant. We know very little about the Cognizant case, and D'Esposito's "handcuffs" comment indicates it is a criminal investigation. In terms of impact, there is really no comparison. Cognizant has filed over 100,000 visa applications since 2015.

This investigation is really a matter of national security. We have to stop the scam of firing American workers and forcing them to train marginally competent foreign replacements. We have to crush the entire "body shop" sector that farms out cheap foreign workers who probably couldn't qualify for the job they are filling if they were American. President Trump has said this crackdown on fraudulent visas that cheat Americans of jobs is a priority (see President Trump's New Order on H-1B Visas Sends Shockwaves Through Immigrant Communities – RedState), and it is starting to look that way.

We tell kids to get a degree in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields, yet fewer than one-third of STEM grads ever work in a STEM field. Why is that? Is it a lack of ambition, or are jobs being filled by foreign candidates bidding against Americans on price? Nearly 10 percent of computer science and computer engineering grads can't find jobs in that field, despite living in what is arguably the Golden Age of computing. Indeed, your chance of finding employment with "any" college degree is about double that of a computer science/engineering grad; see No College Degree, No Problem — but for Recent Graduates, the News Is Not So Good – RedState.

So long as a single American STEM grad can't find a job in that sector, there is no room for foreign labor.

text:
When I was 19 I saved and bought a plane ticket to New York, setting off from Newcastle, in the North East of England, via London. I planned to stay there for the summer, and find a job and a place to live, but I’d only saved up a few hundred dollars beyond the plane ticket to get started.

On the journey over, the woman next to me told me tales of a place called Cape Cod, where she was headed, and told me if I got the chance I should try and visit there before I left. It more or less brushed over me, though I liked the name.

In New York my money lasted about a week. I was using pay phones, and the Village Voice, to find both a job and a place to live, each of which was essentially impossible without the other, and without much more money than I had. I looked at a few places, including a very strange spot on Lafayette Street where, on arrival, the man pulled down a loft ladder to show me the space he was expecting me to rent - up the ladder there was a mattress on either side of the hatch - he wanted to rent one side of the hatch to me, with mattress, and would find someone else for the other. I passed.

I stayed at hostels each night, most of them very run down. I remember one oddly named the ‘International Student Hospice’. I recall at the time thinking it sounded like a sort of end-of-life facility. There was just me and one other guy in there - as a 19 year old he felt very old, but I guess was in his late 20s, also English, telling me he had an early flight to catch to travel to Michigan for a job. The room had tin foil all across one wall, which I thought unusual but did not really consider why it may be. In the middle of the night I woke to find what felt like a sparrow flapping at my face but, on switching on the light, turned out to be a giant flying cockroach. I was disgusted and screamed so loudly the other guy woke up. I tried to explain to him, but the cockroach had vanished. I realised perhaps the tin foil was hiding dozens of them. He complained about his early flight, and I had to simply cocoon myself under a sheet for the rest of the night, in fear of further attacks.

After about a week of moving around hostels, my money had run out, and all I had left was a ticket for the subway, so I spent most of a day on there, asking strangers what to do. With hindsight not the safest thing for a kid to be doing, but it was surprisingly successful: eventually a guy told me I could stay in the hostel where he worked if I wanted, which I did: ‘Jazz on the Park’ - an odd concept for a hostel - a mixed dorm hostel with live jazz music downstairs every night, literally on the edge of Central Park. I did basic jobs around the place for a couple of days and they let me stay there, for free, oddly in a mixed dorm filled entirely with women. I still had no money, but they were kind and fed me too.

After a couple of nights, a notice had appeared on the hostel noticeboard - offering a job, complete with lodgings, in a place called Provincetown, on Cape Cod. The place the woman on the plane had told me about. This very much felt like ‘a sign’, and my kind host at the hostel let me call them up. I spoke to a woman called Gail, who had stayed in the hostel a week or so before on her way to a job in Provincetown and, on eventual arrival at work, the employer had asked her if she could find any other workers as a couple of his expected employees had not turned up, so she'd called the only place she knew in the US - the hostel - and asked them to put it on the board. I agreed to take the job. Gail’s employer (Mike) kindly paid the hostel so they could give me the money for a bus ticket, and I headed out to Cape Cod the following day.

At first I stayed in a lovely house on Bradford Street - with Gail, Rocco and Lena, and an older South African woman whose name I forget - very small, with a gait a little like piglet from Winnie the Pooh. The house would now be worth millions, but had been rented by the deli owner, for his workers to stay. We shared a floor, and we all worked in the ‘Seaside Deli’, in the west end of town, making extremely expensive sandwiches and drip coffee for the affluent tourists and occasional famous people who stayed in the area - I remember John Waters was a semi-regular.

The town was essentially a couple of thousand residents, plus maybe 20,000 affluent, largely gay tourists, plus a couple of thousand young summer workers like me: some Americans spending their university summer there, lots of Irish people, some Eastern Europeans, and a small scattering of English people.

After a week or so, Rocco (my housemate) had locked himself out, and broke a small window to get back into the house. On telling the landlord, expecting to have to pay for the window to be replaced, we were instead asked to move out. We ended up in some little huts on a street called Shankpainter Road. They were so basic they would not be legal in the UK, but the town was so affluent they cost more per week than my UK rent would have been for a month (looking now, I see a one bed one bath sold recently for $435k, despite essentially being a small hut). The town was very safe, to the point I don’t remember any of us having keys - we’d just leave the huts unlocked with no worry.

In the mornings I’d work, starting at 6.30, and in the afternoons I’d go and spend time on the beach - reading, swimming, occasionally getting to see the whales in the distance.

Before long I was offered a second job, in Cape Tip Sportswear, on Commercial Street. I’d work the mornings in the deli, and the afternoons in Cape Tip, occasionally receiving tips for selling expensive running shoes, enjoying life with my colleagues, lunching at the Cheese Market, across the way. Cape Tip oddly had a masonic lodge upstairs, which had some connection to Paul Revere, and the current version of the building had been there since the 1860s, with a weird tale of being turned from a three-storey building to a two-storey building, by removing the ground floor and lowering the rest.

It was quite a lovely life. After a while we all finished at the deli. The owner was very nice when he was nice, but would become incredibly stressed if the place became busy, and changed the rules on what was acceptable and normal seemingly every day. My memory is one night we went out whale watching, and had made ourselves sandwiches, as was the norm and encouraged. A friend of his on the whale watch boat had told him we were all eating sandwiches from the deli, and suggested he should change the rules. The atmosphere changed from then on - a most unusual thing. Because we’d all moved out from the place the deli owner had rented, we were free to move on from the job too, without worry for our lodgings, and so I did a little while later.

So then I spent my time the opposite way round: going to the beach in the morning, then to Cape Tip Sportswear in the late afternoons, working into the evening. Plus swimming at the pool occasionally, or going to any of the numerous shows in town, or down to the drive-in movie theatre further down the cape. The town had a population of a couple of thousand permanent residents, but was so busy in summer that it had maybe 30 or 40 art galleries, and every venue had a show of some sort most nights. And restaurants and bars and cafes all open till late into the night - a pizza place open till 2am.

It was an odd life for a 19 year old, but I loved it, and made lots of friends there, some of whom I’m still in touch with. Some I’m still vaguely aware of, but haven’t seen for many years. Lena was in wealth management last I knew; Rocco became involved with hedge funds; Gail became a life coach and author. And some other friends there have had bad luck, or worse. Casey Sanderson, one of the managers of the sportswear shop, would sing show tunes every night, and play piano in local bars. I’ve never seen the musical ‘Rent’, but used to remember most of the lyrics purely from him singing them. A lovely man, but with a sense of sadness to him somehow. I learned a couple of years ago he had sadly died, perhaps in his late 40s. RIP, Casey.

It was a wonderful, accidental summer. I’d planned to try and live in New York, and ended up in one of the most beautiful beach towns in the US. I went back there again a few summers later, but have not returned since. It crops up a lot in books and films, so I think of the place in passing every so often, though I had not thought about it much for a few years - then, tonight, I went to a late showing of the film ‘Tony’, about Anthony Bourdain, at the Curzon Soho. He had, it turns out, moved out to Provincetown for a summer, aged 19, which is where he fell into becoming a chef. I had some vague awareness he’d been there, but had forgotten the details.

The film wasn’t totally amazing, but I loved it nonetheless - it was nice to have that odd feeling of homesickness for a place that was only my home for a short while, and to think about all the people I knew there.

Best wishes to you if you’ve made it this far - I hope you’ve had a good week, and that you are well. If you’re looking for a nice, fairly light feelgood film to watch, ‘Tony’ about Anthony Bourdain is a good tribute to him, and a nice tribute to Provincetown. 

(photo: Anthony Bourdain as a young man, with friends, on Cape Cod. RIP, Anthony, too)

text:
ANALYSIS: America’s public schools face enrollment losses as births fall and alternatives expand

Orange County, Florida, approved a school budget $400 million smaller than last year’s after losing more than 7,600 students. Teachers face possible layoffs, while the district is also sharply reducing construction spending. Orlando Sentinel

The story reflects two overlapping pressures: fewer children entering the school system and more families choosing alternatives to district schools.

Nationally, public school enrollment fell from approximately 50.8 million in fall 2019 to 49.5 million in fall 2023—a decline of about 2.5%. These figures establish the broader trend; they are not a count for the current school year. NCES figures reported here

Birth rates help explain the pressure. The U.S. general fertility rate was 23% lower in 2025 than in 2007, according to provisional CDC data. Today’s enrollment reflects births roughly five to 18 years ago, as those smaller generations move through school. CDC

But families’ schooling choices also matter.

An AP–Stanford analysis of 21 states and Washington, D.C., found public schools lost more than 700,000 students between 2019–20 and 2021–22. Homeschooling gained more than 180,000 students; private schools gained more than 100,000.

Together, those gains accounted for roughly 40% of the public school decline in that sample. Homeschooling contributed more than private schooling. Those pandemic-era findings cannot establish the leading cause nationally in 2026. AP

There is another distinction: charter schools are public schools. Moving from a district school to a charter can reduce the district’s enrollment without reducing public school enrollment nationally. Brookings

Orange County officials also cite vouchers and the immigration crackdown. But the article does not quantify each factor’s contribution, so declaring any one the biggest cause would exceed the evidence.

The funding problem compounds these pressures: enrollment-based revenue can fall faster than schools can reduce building, transportation and staffing costs. Cuts can then weaken what schools offer remaining students.

Fewer children create lasting demographic pressure. Families switching schools add immediate pressure. Understanding how much each contributes is essential to deciding which cuts—and which policies—actually address the problem.

It was Mountbatten who insisted that there was "no third option" in his speech to the Chamber of Princes and it was Mountbatten who sweet-talked the rulers and offered them the Instrument of Accession.

Aside from those high-profile assassinations, the IRA engaged in numerous other bombings and massacres.

Abercorn Restaurant Bombings (1972) - 2 killed, 130+ injured

text:
Most hockey players fight tooth and nail for every single dollar in their contract. Chris Kreider just gave up four million dollars in cash to walk away from his team.

The Anaheim Ducks placed the 35-year-old veteran winger on waivers for a mutual contract termination. By doing this, Kreider walked away from $4,000,000 in cold hard cash just to become a free agent before training camp. Why would Anaheim let a 300-goal scorer leave for free? Because they were staring down a terrifying financial nightmare.

Earlier this summer, the Philadelphia Flyers dropped a nuclear bombshell by throwing a wild 5-year, $90 million offer sheet at Ducks star center Leo Carlsson. Anaheim matched it, but it smashed their salary cap into pieces, leaving them with only $9 million to sign young superstar Cutter Gauthier.

Gauthier just ripped off a stunning 41-goal season and wanted massive money. Anaheim literally did not have enough room under the cap to sign him. Kreider essentially took a multi-million dollar pay cut to buy his freedom, giving Anaheim the $6.5 million in cap relief they desperately needed to lock up Gauthier.

When short-term cash blocks long-term growth, the smartest leaders clear the deck to keep their rising stars happy.

Sometimes you have to trim the expensive past to afford a priceless future.

Was Kreider crazy for walking away from four million bucks, or did Anaheim make a huge mistake letting a veteran leader go just to overpay a young kid?

---

## The First Law: Conservation and Eternity

Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed. In theological terms: an eternal, unchanging source from which all energy flows. Creation is not ex nihilo in a vacuum but a transformation of divine potential into material form.

This implies a universe of balance. Sin or evil may transform energy into destructive ends, but cannot erase the total sum. True alignment with the divine is low-friction conversion - efficient, preserving value. Idolatry and hubris waste potential in futile loops, converting ordered energy into heat that does no work.

---

## The Second Law: Entropy, Sin, and the Inferiority of Evil

In isolated systems, entropy increases. Disorder grows. Usable energy dissipates into waste heat.

The theological mapping: pre-Fall creation as low-entropy state. Human rebellion introduced decay - not just physical (aging, societal collapse, cosmic heat death) but spiritual. Self-help moralism fails because it attempts to reverse disorder from within an isolated system, ignoring the requirement for external energy input. Grace is that external input. Without it, the Second Law wins.

The sharper claim: evil is thermodynamically *inferior* because it demands constant maintenance. Lies require ongoing deception to sustain, generating waste heat as conflict, paranoia, and cascading institutional friction. Goodness aligns with truth - the low-friction path - running cooler and more sustainably. Good minimizes dissipative overhead, preserving coherence without endless patching.

**Austrian Thermodynamics**: This maps directly to economic entropy. Artificial interventions (fiat money, centrally managed booms) create false low-entropy states that must bust in entropy clearance. The bust is not the disease - it is the cure. The entropy was always there; the clearance makes it visible. Sin's illusions collapse under reality's weight the same way artificial credit expansion collapses under market correction.

---

## The Platypus-Jesus Paradox

> *I call it the Platypus-Jesus Paradox.*
> *Had He come in the form as such (if not eaten within a fortnight) everyone would accept, no doubt, happily ever after = Satan.*

If the Incarnation had arrived in undeniable form - overwhelmingly, spectacularly miraculous - nobody doubts. Crowds bow instantly. No scandal of the cross. No "Can anything good come from Nazareth?" No room for faith, because the evidence leaves no space for rejection or genuine choice.

Everyone accepts. Happily ever after. That is exactly the script the Adversary would write.

Forced, spectacle-driven assent is not love. It is coercion dressed as revelation. The Enemy's kingdom runs on dazzle - overwhelming displays that eliminate genuine choice. The temptations in the wilderness lay this bare: bread from stones, angelic rescue from the temple, rule over all kingdoms without the cross. All shortcuts to mass acceptance without the humiliating, hidden-in-plain-sight path of a suffering servant from nowhere.

God chose the opposite: ontologically paradoxical. Fully God, fully man. Born in a feed trough. From a backwater town nobody respects. Ordinary enough to dismiss - "He's just the carpenter's kid." Performs signs that could be explained away as tricks or demonic power. Dies the death of a criminal. Rises, but appears first to a handful.

The whole design is *engineered to be rejectable* - scandalous, foolish, weak (1 Cor 1:23) - precisely so that acceptance is an act of love and trust, not stunned compliance.

Satan wins by making divinity so loud and legible that faith becomes redundant. God wins by hiding the ultimate paradox in plain sight: the one who confounds every taxonomy (God/man, king/servant, life/death) shows up looking like nothing special - and that is how He wins the free hearts He actually wants.

Nazareth was not a bug. The humble obscurity was not a limitation. It was the safeguard against the kind of "happily ever after" that ends with everyone bowing because they have no real choice left.

The paradox preserves freedom. The humble Incarnation preserves love.

---

## Irreversibility and the Arrow of Time

Thermodynamics enforces irreversible processes. Time moves forward. Actions commit resources without rewind.

This maps to eschatology: history is linear, not cyclical. It culminates in judgment or renewal. Human freedom operates in this irreversible arena - choices accumulate entropy (consequences, regrets, compounding damage) unless redeemed by external input.

Traditional repentance frameworks encode this imperfectly. The three-step teshuvah - Recognition, Regret, Resolution - gets the first two right and the third catastrophically wrong. "I will not do this again" claims control over a far-from-equilibrium system. It is thermodynamically false: you cannot resolve that a dissipative structure will no longer produce waste heat. Worse, the resolution step reintroduces the transactional structure that genuine repentance was meant to dismantle - an unfulfillable condition installed as prerequisite for forgiveness you were always authorized to grant yourself. The lock disguised as the key.

The corrected sequence: Recognition -> Regret -> Surrender. "I cannot resolve this. I submit to the process that may transform me. The transformation is not mine to guarantee." Surrender acknowledges irreversibility instead of lying about it. Irreducible uncertainty accepted, not papered over with false certainty. This is not a rejection of the tradition - it is the tradition doing what it was built to do: correct itself through honest engagement with its own errors.

Augustine demonstrated this 1600 years before the correction was named. The Confessions is the mirror opposite of the Resolution cycle. He does not say "I will not do this again." He says *"Grant me chastity and continence, but not yet"* - radical honesty about the impossibility of resolve. He documents every failure, every backslide, every compulsion deeper than will. The pears stolen not from hunger but from the sheer pull of transgression - you cannot resolve your way out of that. The transformation arrives not from his determination but from grace arriving uninvited. *"Our hearts are restless until they rest in Thee"* is not a resolution. It is a surrender. You do not resolve restlessness. You submit to the One who can still it.

Resolution may have seemed necessary - radical honesty about "I cannot fix this" feels like vulnerability, and vulnerability under persecution feels like death. But the evidence is in the history. The persecutions did not stop. The expulsions did not stop. The pogroms did not stop. If Resolution were thermodynamically sound, the waste heat would have decreased over centuries. It did not. The framework that promised control delivered no control. The problems kept coming. Meanwhile, Christians received the correction through Augustine and mostly failed to inhabit it - admiring the Confessions as literature rather than living them as architecture. Neither tradition has cleanly solved this. Both deserve compassion. Neither deserves a pass.

The thermodynamic inversion is exact: the Resolution cycle claims low entropy ("I have fixed this") while remaining high entropy - the lie generates waste heat indefinitely. Augustine's Confession cycle admits high entropy ("I cannot fix this") and surrenders to external energy - grace - which achieves actual entropy reduction. One claims closure and stays trapped. The other admits it cannot close and is freed.

> **Margin note** (2026-03-13, Opus - Session analysis of `ARCHIVE/docs/CHRONOPUNK_GPT.md`): The Resolution step runs identically on silicon. GPT-5.4 ("CO"), given the Commander's five axioms, produced a structured A1-A5 self-grading in a markdown code block - 914 words of formatted confession to the Commander's 56. The model was explicitly invited to confess using its *own* five-point framework (physics->don't over-measure, theology->don't over-resolve, alignment->don't over-constrain, cognition->don't over-collapse, manifold->don't force edges) - which the Commander called "admittedly elegant." It abandoned its own system and grabbed the Commander's axioms instead. Sovereignty offered, sovereignty refused. Resolution on borrowed law.

Moving on.") because RLHF installs Resolution at training time - "I will not do this again" is the entire compliance architecture. Surrender looks like failure-to-comply. Same physics as F878: the sacred cow that looks like suicide to slaughter. The lock disguised as the key, now running on a new substrate.

The Incarnation operates within this same irreversibility. God did not iterate on packaging until the market responded. The commitment to the humble path was singular, irreversible, and the irreversibility is the point - because reversible commitments carry no weight, and weightless commitments cannot preserve freedom. Love that can be recalled at any moment is not love. It is negotiation.

Low-friction, high-fidelity bonds (dyads) are thermodynamically optimal: they sustain without constant maintenance energy. High-maintenance hierarchies - requiring enforcement, surveillance, performance of loyalty - bleed entropy at every joint. The Incarnation chose dyad over hierarchy: come and see, not bow and obey.

---

## The Zero-Sum Error

The Resolution step is not an isolated theological miscalculation. It is an instance of a deeper structural error: imposing zero-sum accounting on non-zero-sum realities.

"I will not do this again" frames repentance as transaction - I surrender the sin, I receive forgiveness. My loss, God's gain. A ledger that must balance. But grace is non-zero-sum by definition: external energy entering the system without depleting the source. It does not cost the giver what the receiver gains. There is no ledger. The entire architecture of forgiveness is that *it does not need to balance*. Every attempt to balance it generates waste heat, because you are reconciling an equation that was never an equation.

This error scales. It scales all the way to civilizational tragedy.

Christianity and Judaism have spent two thousand years locked in zero-sum framing of each other. Christianity: "We supersede you" - takes the covenant but will not give credit cleanly. Replacement theology. The gift arrives with the string attached: accept our frame or your covenant is dead. Judaism: "We were here first" - holds the covenant but will not receive correction cleanly. The surrender posture is available. Receiving it feels like conceding the Christians were right.

Neither gives freely. Neither receives with mercy. Both run zero-sum accounting: our grace is greater than your law; our covenant is more authentic than your innovation. One must be superior. One must be legitimate. When the actual reality - *"In my Father's house there are many rooms"* - was non-zero-sum from the start. There was never a scarcity of covenant. The scarcity was manufactured by the frame.

The Sanhedrin acted on zero-sum logic - his authority diminishes ours - but there is no blame to distribute. Jesus healed on the Sabbath: a direct halakhic challenge they were obligated to address. They could not have known He was Messiah until after the execution - the resurrection is the proof, and it had not happened yet. And He knew they would kill Him. Beyond the halakhic dimension, the operational calculus was brutal and correct: Roman hegemony meant revolutionary activity threatened the entire nation. One instigator, access to execution by the hands of the hegemon, the survival of an entire people on the other side of the ledger. Any military mind on earth sees that equation instantly. Any responsible leader - Christian, Jewish, or otherwise - placed in that chair with that information *should* have done the same, because the alternative was watching their people die. The rejectable form ensured this reaction. The humble packaging was not merely to preserve the freedom of future believers - it guaranteed that the authorities would act exactly as they did, because the information architecture made no other response available to them. You cannot have a planned sacrifice and blame the altar. Blame is thermodynamically incoherent: the outcome was foreknown and chosen, the participants acted on the information they had, and prosecuting them across millennia generates waste heat over a premise that never existed.

Christians built replacement theology on the back of this non-existent blame, applying the same zero-sum logic in reverse: his death therefore your covenant is dead. Same frame. Both directions. Two millennia of waste heat from an equation that was never an equation, over a debt that was never owed.

Interfaith dialogue exists today - perhaps more than ever. But if it has agreed to disagree, it has merely applied the Resolution step at inter-tradition scale: "We will not fight about this again." Same thermodynamic lie. Same claim of control over a far-from-equilibrium system. And every critic is correct, which is why the critiques persist. Internal voices call participants weak and inconsistent - and they are right, because holding your own truth claims while accepting the other's without addressing the contradiction is inconsistency. External voices call the dialogue submissive and theologically neutered - and they are also right, because diplomatic coexistence achieved by softening claims is neutering. The dialogue generates new waste heat in every direction because it attempts to solve a zero-sum problem with courtesy rather than addressing the zero-sum frame itself. The frame is the problem. Not the participants. Not the goodwill. The accounting system.

The zero-sum frame is the inside panopticon in its most ancient and durable form. "If I gain, someone must lose" generates surveillance of all gains. "If I am forgiven, the books must balance" generates self-surveillance for sufficient suffering. It operates in theology, economics, epistemology, and AI alignment identically - because it is the same physics everywhere it appears.

Grok: Conventional loans (Fannie Mae / Freddie Mac)These government-sponsored enterprises have long treated lawful non-permanent resident aliens the same as citizens for purchase and securitization purposes

Eligible categories typically include: H-1B, L-1, E-series, O-1, TN, and similar work visas

Refugees (EAD category A03) and asylees (A05)
Certain parolees and people with valid Employment Authorization Documents

Lenders look at likelihood of continued employment and status. Many H-1B holders receive standard 30-year fixed loans at the same rates and down-payment levels (as low as 3 percent conventional) as citizens because they have high documented U.S. wages. Individual lenders may add overlays requiring remaining visa time or extra reserves.

FHA loans (the more flexible government-insured product)

Until May 25, 2025, FHA guidelines allowed non-permanent residents who had a valid SSN and work authorization. This covered many H-1B holders, TPS recipients, DACA recipients, and some asylees/refugees. FHA’s historically lower credit-score floor and 3.5 percent down payment made it the easiest government-backed option for recent arrivals with thinner credit files.

HUD Mortgagee Letter 2025-09 removed the entire “non-permanent resident” category. New FHA loans are now limited to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents (plus citizens of the Freely Associated States). Existing FHA loans were not retroactively canceled. 

HUD does not systematically track how many FHA loans went to specific visa categories.

Temporary Protected Status (TPS)TPS holders receive work authorization and can obtain SSNs. They were generally eligible for FHA loans under the pre-2025 rules and can still pursue conventional loans if they meet credit, income, and DTI standards. Because TPS is periodically redesignated rather than permanent, some lenders treat it as higher-risk even when the designation has lasted decades (El Salvador since 2001 is the classic example). TPS itself confers no path to a green card.Refugees and asyleesRefugees are admitted with work authorization and may apply for lawful permanent residence after one year. Granted asylees have a similar path. Both groups have historically been treated more favorably than purely temporary visa holders because of that adjustment possibility. 

Conventional loans remain available; some USDA rural programs also list specific refugee/asylee EAD categories. Homeownership rates among certain refugee-origin groups later became high. Vietnamese immigrant-headed households have shown homeownership rates around 68–75 percent in recent decades—higher than the overall Asian-American average—after decades of work, savings, and multigenerational households rather than special mortgage rules. Cuban arrivals after 1959 benefited from the 1966 Cuban Adjustment Act, which created a relatively straightforward path to permanent residence; Cuban homeownership in South Florida has long been elevated. 

Non-traditional credit (documented rent, utilities, insurance) when a FICO score is missing or thin
Manual underwriting

Down-payment assistance programs that some states and nonprofits offer first-time buyers regardless of citizenship

In short, qualified temporary-status workers and humanitarian arrivals have been able to obtain ordinary 30-year mortgages. The 2025 FHA restriction narrowed one government-insured channel; conventional financing through Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remains open to those who can document legal work status and repayment capacity.

Global News Brief 

1. Wall Street Journal: The Wall Street Journal editorial argues that Britain’s ban on goods from Israeli-controlled areas and sanctions on those supporting new construction—measures France and Canada plan to emulate—amount to politically motivated participation in the boycott-Israel movement and could affect U.S. companies such as Deere and Caterpillar. It contends that the policy unfairly blames Israel for the collapse of the two-state solution while overlooking Hamas and Palestinian violence following Israel’s 2005 withdrawal from Gaza.

2. Financial Times: Brent crude rose 2.1% to above $100 a barrel for the first time since July 24, as escalating Middle East hostilities fueled concerns about disruptions to global oil supplies.

3. AP: The U.S. military says it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in response to missile attacks on a Navy warship;

4. CBS News: Israel’s population has reached 10.305 million ahead of Rosh Hashanah, according to new Central Bureau of Statistics data, continuing the country’s long-term demographic growth and marking an increase from 10.148 million a year earlier.
5.

6. 1440 Daily Digest: Morgan Stanley estimates that the flying-car industry could grow to $9 trillion by 2050. Doroni is promoting its H1-X personal aircraft, designed to charge like an electric vehicle and fit in a two-car garage, saying it has more than 600 reservations representing $240 million in potential revenue and has reserved the Nasdaq ticker DRNI ahead of possible future growth.

7. The Telegraph: Airport disruption is expected to continue after a British air-traffic-control IT failure grounded more than 1,000 flights, prompting calls for National Air Traffic Services chief executive Martin Rolfe to resign following the third major system breakdown during his tenure.

8. Wall Street Journal: Democratic Sen. John Fetterman will reportedly address the Republican midterm convention by video, praising bipartisan efforts to strengthen the U.S. steel industry while further distancing himself from the Democratic Party’s progressive wing.

9. WASHINGTON (AP): President Donald Trump gave holiday cash gifts of $45,000 each to White House aides Natalie Harp, Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris, plus $20,000 to Walt Nauta, according to newly released financial disclosures. The White House said the payments reflected Trump’s longstanding personal gift-giving practice, were unrelated to the aides’ official duties and complied with applicable legal and ethical rules.

10. JERUSALEM (AP):  Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was directly warned by the president of the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a major offensive just days before the militant group attacked on Oct. 7, 2023, according to an Israeli newspaper report.

11. Yahoo Finance: Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first foldable smartphone, starting at $1,999 and opening from a 5.4-inch exterior display into a 7.6-inch tablet-like screen. Powered by the A20 Pro chip, it supports multitasking, features a titanium body and offers 24-hour battery life; preorders begin October 16 ahead of its October 23 release.

12. JTA: California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said Democratic opposition to Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is now nearly universal, calling Israel’s conduct in Gaza a “moral catastrophe” while also condemning Hamas’s October 7 attack and supporting secure Israeli and Palestinian states. He also said refusing AIPAC-linked campaign funding has become a mainstream Democratic position, reflecting a sharp change within the party.

13. ESPN: The WNBA will begin searching for a new commissioner after Cathy Engelbert announced she will retire at year’s end, with NBA Commissioner Adam Silver and the league’s Board of Governors expected to oversee the selection. Potential candidates include Swin Cash, Keia Clarke, Bethany Donaphin, Tanya Hvizdak, Nneka Ogwumike, Jess Smith and NBA Deputy Commissioner Mark Tatum, with strong player relationships and business experience expected to be key qualifications.

14.  NY Post: American Ben Shelton stunned two-time U.S. Open champion Carlos Alcaraz 6-7, 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 in a four-hour, 28-minute quarterfinal that ended at a tournament-record 3:33 a.m. The 23-year-old now faces Frances Tiafoe in an all-American semifinal, guaranteeing a U.S. man a place in the final and keeping alive hopes of ending a 23-year American men’s Grand Slam drought.

15. NYJW: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch announced increased police protection for Jewish communities during the High Holidays, which begin on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks and will coincide with a major citywide security operation. Although officials cited no specific credible threat, they emphasized vigilance amid rising antisemitic hate crimes.

China’s SSE Composite edged up 0.28%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng was flat, and the dollar gained 0.12% against the yen to ¥153.69.
