text:
I read your article carefully. And I have to say: it is a masterclass in historical manipulation. You take a few facts, strip them of context, and build a narrative that erases an entire people. Let me show you what you left out.

You repeat a familiar Zionist talking point: (There was never a Palestinian state.) But this is a distraction, not an argument. It confuses the absence of a modern sovereign state with the absence of a historically continuous people. And it uses that confusion to deny the political rights of the Palestinians.

Let us be clear from the start: The Palestinian people did not need to establish a sovereign republic in 1596 in order for Palestinian society to exist in Palestine. The Ottoman state’s own fiscal archives prove that.

The Ottoman administration produced detailed tahrir registers for taxation and administration. These records documented villages, households, agricultural production, land use, religious communities, and taxes. The significance is precisely that these were not Palestinian nationalist documents. They were created by an imperial government for its own administrative and fiscal purposes. The Ottoman state had no reason to invent a Palestinian population. It was simply recording the people it governed.

The sixteenth-century Ottoman records, including the detailed register of 1596, document hundreds of Palestinian villages and their households, agricultural production, and tax obligations. Ottoman records for cities including Jerusalem, Hebron, Gaza, Ramla, Nablus, and Safed also allow historians to reconstruct the religious and demographic composition of Palestinian urban society.

What do these records show?

A large, settled, Arabic-speaking Muslim and Christian population – the ancestors of today’s Palestinians – lived in towns and villages across the country. They paid taxes, cultivated the land, and owned property. They were the demographic majority. Jews were a longstanding but small minority, like Christians and Samaritans.

So when you ask (Where were the Palestinians before 1948?) the answer is simple: They were in the towns and villages that the Ottoman government was registering, administering, and taxing centuries before the Zionist movement existed.

Now ask the opposite question: Where were the Jews before 1948?

Where did the 367,845 Jewish immigrants who arrived between 1920 and 1945 come from? The answer is in the official British Mandate table, Table 1 from (A Survey of Palestine.)

Look at the numbers.

Between 1920 and 1945, 367,845 Jews immigrated to Palestine. In 1925 alone, 33,801 Jews arrived – over 39% of all immigrants that year. In 1934, 42,359 Jews arrived – over 95% of all immigrants. In 1935, 61,854 Jews arrived – over 96% of all immigrants.

These were not (returning) to the land of their ancestors. These were immigrants from Eastern and Central Europe, where they had been living before the war. In 1925, most came from Poland and Russia. In 1934, most came from Germany, Austria, and Czechoslovakia. In 1935, most came from Poland, Romania, and Germany.

They were Europeans. Their language was Yiddish, German, Polish. Their culture was European. They were not Middle Eastern. They were not Palestinian.

Meanwhile, the Palestinians – Muslims and Christians – were living in their towns and villages, farming their land, and paying taxes to the Ottoman state, then to the British Mandate. They did not come from anywhere. They were already there.

So the question is not (Where was the Palestinian state?) The question is (Where were the Jews before 1948?) The answer: in Europe. And they came to Palestine. The Palestinians did not go anywhere – they stayed in their homeland.

That is the difference between an indigenous people and a settler population. The difference between continuous presence and settler colonialism.

Now, let us be precise about 1948 and 1967. Your article confuses three different historical moments. Let us separate them.

1948: The Nakba.

In 1948, Israel seized control of 78% of historic Palestine. Jordan took control of the West Bank and East Jerusalem. Egypt took control of Gaza. And in the process, over 750,000 Palestinians were expelled or forced from their homes, and over 530 villages were destroyed.

The question is not (Was there a Palestinian state?) The question is: On what legal basis were hundreds of thousands of Palestinians expelled or forced from their homes in 1947–49?

There is no legal basis. The Nakba was not a (war of independence.) It was ethnic cleansing. Israeli historians like Ilan Pappé and Benny Morris have documented this. The expulsions were deliberate, systematic, and planned.

1948–1967: Jordanian and Egyptian control.

From 1948 to 1967, the West Bank was under Jordanian control, and Gaza was under Egyptian control. Neither was a Palestinian state. But that does not mean the Palestinians had no rights. They were still the indigenous population of those territories.

1967: The Occupation.

In 1967, Israel occupied the West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem, the Golan Heights, and the Sinai Peninsula. This was not (liberation.) It was a military occupation, illegal under international law.

You claim Israel fought a (defensive war) in 1967 and that it had no intention of conquering the West Bank, Gaza, or the Golan Heights. But the Israeli military’s own archives prove you wrong.

The plans existed before the war.

According to the official archive of the Israel Defense Forces, by late May 1967 – before a single shot was fired – the Israeli military had already prepared detailed operational plans for multiple fronts: (Kardom) for the destruction of the Egyptian air force and the Egyptian army in Sinai, dated May 10, 1967. (Atzmon) for the occupation of the Gaza Strip, dated May 20, 1967. (Pargol) for the occupation of the West Bank, dated May 30, 1967. And (Makevet) for the occupation of the Golan Heights.

The IDF archive itself states: (Until the outbreak of the war, June 5, these plans and orders were modified according to the developments.)

So the question is not (Did Israel plan to occupy these territories?) The question is: If Israel was only fighting a defensive war, why did it already have operational plans to conquer the West Bank, Gaza, and the Golan Heights – before the war even started?

The preparations were not improvised.

Declassified Israeli documents from the Israel State Archives and the IDF Archives reveal that the takeover and retention of these areas were not a (by-product of the fighting) but (the manifestation of a strategic approach and prior preparations.) The IDF’s meticulous planning to conquer these territories had already begun in the early 1960s.

In June 1961, six years before the war, the IDF’s head of operations prepared a document titled (Proposal to Organize the Military Government) – detailed planning for the forces that would be needed to rule the occupied territories.

By August 1963, the IDF General Staff Branch, then headed by Yitzhak Rabin, issued a directive regarding (the organization of the military government in the territories.) This order explicitly identified Israel’s (expected directions of expansion,) which included the West Bank, Sinai, the Syrian Heights, and southern Lebanon up to the Litani River.

The order stated: (The IDF’s thrust to transfer the war to the enemy’s territories will necessarily bring about expansion into and conquest of areas beyond the state’s borders.)

It even hinted at the intention to retain occupied territory: (However, a convenient political situation might develop which will make it possible to retain occupied territory indefinitely.)

Israeli generals admitted the plan.

In 1972, General Mordechai Hod – whose forces destroyed the Egyptian, Syrian, and Jordanian air forces on June 5, 1967 – declared: (For sixteen years, we had been planning what took place in those first 80 minutes. We lived with that plan, we ate with it, we slept with it. We never stopped improving it.)

As early as 1955, Chief of Staff Moshe Dayan explained that Israel would have no difficulty finding a pretext for attacking Egypt: (We should be ready to conquer the Gaza Strip... and we should think of a triple-stage plan... As to Jordan, there is a two-stage plan: the first is to reach the Hebron line. The second is to take the rest of the territory up to the Jordan River.)

So let us be clear about 1967. The war did not begin because Israel faced an (existential threat.) It began because Israel had a plan to expand its borders, and the crisis provided the pretext.

And on what legal basis did those planned military conquests become Israeli territory?

There is none. UN Security Council Resolution 242, passed in 1967, explicitly calls for (the withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict.) Resolution 338, passed in 1973, reaffirms this. Resolution 2334, passed in 2016, states that Israeli settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem are a (flagrant violation) of international law and have (no legal validity.)

Israel has no legal claim to the West Bank, Gaza, or East Jerusalem. These are occupied Palestinian territories. The settlements are illegal. The occupation is illegal. The siege of Gaza is illegal. The apartheid system is illegal.

Your legal argument collapses.

You repeatedly move from (There was no sovereign Palestinian state) to (Therefore Israel inherited sovereignty over the entire territory of Mandatory Palestine.) That conclusion does not follow. You still have to establish the missing legal step.

Where exactly did international law transfer sovereignty over the whole of Mandatory Palestine to the Jewish people?

Not a promise of a (national home.) Not historical Jewish attachment. Not the fact that the Ottoman Empire previously ruled the territory. Not Jordan’s subsequent illegal annexation. And not the mere existence of British administrative boundaries.

Show the actual legal instrument that transferred sovereignty over the entire territory to Israel. Because neither the Balfour Declaration nor the Mandate itself was a deed transferring Palestine to the Jewish people. And uti possidetis juris does not allow you to simply declare that an entire former Mandate automatically became Israeli territory upon the declaration of independence. That is precisely the proposition you need to prove rather than assume.

You say (Jordan occupied the West Bank.)

Jordan annexed the West Bank in 1950, after Israel expelled its Palestinian population. The annexation was recognized only by Britain and Pakistan. The international community has consistently considered the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, occupied Palestinian territory. UN Security Council resolutions 242, 338, and 2334 all confirm this.

You say (settlements are legal.)

Settlements are illegal under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, which prohibits the transfer of civilians into occupied territory. UN Security Council resolutions 452, 465, and 2334 all confirm this. The International Court of Justice ruled in 2004 that the wall Israel built in the West Bank is illegal.

You say (Palestinians rejected every offer.)

This is a gross simplification. Camp David 2000 did not offer real sovereignty over Jerusalem or a just solution for refugees. Olmert’s 2008 offer was better but still insufficient. Palestinians did not reject (a state.) They rejected a state without real sovereignty.

You say (the right of return is a myth.)

The right of return is enshrined in UN General Assembly Resolution 194, passed in 1948, which states that Palestinian refugees who wish to return to their homes and live in peace with their neighbors should be permitted to do so at the earliest practicable date. Israel has refused to implement this resolution for 75 years.

The Ottoman archives prove that Palestine was not an empty land. It was a populated, administered, and taxed country, with established towns, villages, landholders, and communities centuries before the State of Israel existed. The Palestinians are the descendants of that population. They have the right to self-determination, the right to return, and the right to live in their homeland free from occupation and apartheid.

Recognizing that historical continuity does not require denying Jewish history. But Jewish history cannot be converted retroactively into exclusive modern sovereignty simply by inserting the phrase (international law) into the argument.

I am not writing this as an academic exercise. I am writing this as a Palestinian. My family was among those 750,000. My village is among those 530. And no amount of legal sophistry or historical revisionism will change that.

We were here before you. We are here now. And we will be here long after your occupation ends.

So let me ask you one final question: If you truly believe in justice, why are you defending an occupation that denies the basic rights of millions of people? If you truly believe in international law, why do you ignore the rulings of the very bodies you cite? And if you truly believe in peace, why do you defend a system that makes peace impossible?

This flight line at the El Alamein Airshow 2026 offers an incredible concentration of Egyptian air power. From Ka-52 attack helicopters and F-16s to MiG-29s, Mirages and a wide range of special-mission aircraft, the sheer depth on display is striking.

That is the scale largely missing from Sub-Saharan African air forces. In absolute terms, the only two Black African air forces that come remotely close are the South African and Nigerian Air Forces.

South Africa has quality fighter capabilities with its Gripen fleet and considerable potential, but its Air Force has been scaled down significantly in the absence of a pressing security imperative.

Nigeria is in a different position. It has developed considerable strength in rotary wing aviation, surveillance and special mission platforms, and COIN capabilities given its security imperative.

If Nigeria can build an Air Force approaching the scale and breadth of the major North African powers, the benefits would extend far beyond Nigeria. A substantially larger and more capable Nigerian Air Force would strengthen deterrence, regional security and the overall security architecture of West Africa.

text:
Thursday morning headlines from #Georgia, 10 September

● According to a study by Transparency International Georgia, the privatisation of state-owned property in the Adjara region is often carried out without competition and in favour of people linked to the ruling Georgian Dream party. According to the organisation, 54 of 69 electronic auctions announced since January 2025 failed to attract bidders, while in eight of the 15 successful auctions, the property was sold without competitors. The study found that the owners of winning companies and their family members donated a total of 1.387 million lari (about $500,000) to the ruling party, while two companies received more than 59.5 million lari (about $23 million) in state tenders. The region received just 4.5 million lari (about $1.7 million) from privatisation, against a planned 125 million lari (about $48 million) — just 3.6% of the target.

● Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili says that “no one in the world is saying anymore that convicted journalist Mzia Amaglobeli is innocent”, and that international statements now concern only the proportionality of her sentence — two years in prison for slapping a police officer who had insulted her. According to Papuashvili, Amaglobeli was offered a plea deal, which she rejected. He called the founder of the popular Netgazeti and Batumelebi outlets “a prisoner of the opposition and Brussels’ dishonesty” and accused foreign diplomats of strengthening her position.

● The Georgian Orthodox Church is distancing itself from the creation of a “Father Gabriel Urgebadze unit” in the Russian armed forces and the use of the saint’s name. Andria Jagmaidze, a representative of the Patriarchate, said the Georgian Church had not been consulted on the matter. He also said it was concerning that some Russian Orthodox clergy had supported the initiative.

Earlier, reports emerged that a “Father Gabriel Urgebadze unit” was taking part in fighting against Ukraine, with the support of “Georgian public figure Besik Danelia” and including “Georgian volunteers”. The information was disseminated by Russian state news agency RIA Novosti.

● Former Georgian Prosecutor General Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze said he decided to join Russia’s war against Ukraine after Vladimir Putin invited him to the May 9, 2025 Victory Day parade. According to Partskhaladze, he served for nine months in the Arbat volunteer corps before creating an international volunteer unit, Georgievski, together with his associates. Partskhaladze also said he was proud of the Western sanctions imposed on him, comparing them to an “Order of Truth”. He said members of Georgievski “will defend Russia against the West”, which he accused of “oppressing traditional family, culture and identity”. More here https://t.co/oTEk3gvvj4

● Imprisoned former president Mikheil Saakashvili commented on letters sharply criticising the authorities that are also being published by imprisoned former prime minister Irakli Gharibashvili. Saakashvili said the former prime minister was so far only “gently warning Bidzina Ivanishvili” — honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party and an oligarch widely seen as Georgia’s de facto ruler. According to Saakashvili, Gharibashvili would cause real harm to Ivanishvili if he began speaking about possible crimes of which he himself has information. Saakashvili also called on members of the ruling team to disclose information about Ivanishvili.

● A private plane flying from Batumi to Turkey made an emergency landing in the Black Sea after an engine failure. The plane landed about four nautical miles off the coast of Rize province. The two Belgian citizens on board were rescued by the Turkish coast guard. Neither was injured, and both were taken to hospital for examination.

● The Tbilisi Court of Appeals rejected an appeal by prominent animal rights activist and businessman Tamaz Elizbarashvili and kept him in custody. Prosecutors accuse Elizbarashvili of threatening his opponent with death and physical violence during a conflict in Tbilisi on August 30. Elizbarashvili denies the charges and went on hunger strike after his arrest.

● According to a report by the PMC Research Center, the volume of transit cargo passing through Georgia fell by 9.5% in 2025, from 15.1 million tonnes to 13.7 million tonnes. The main reason was a 7.8% decline in cargo flows along the East-West corridor, which accounts for almost 70% of Georgia’s transit cargo. Cargo turnover along the corridor fell by 33.5%, reaching its lowest level since 2019.

● A 6.5 million lari (about $2.5 million) tender has been announced to prepare design documentation for the reconstruction of the Tbilisi Philharmonic Hall. The project includes improving the hall’s acoustics, inspecting stage equipment, modernising lifts, upgrading the security system and making the building accessible to people with disabilities. The existing screen on the main façade is also to be removed.

● Education Minister Givi Mikanadze met Ukrainian Education and Science Minister Andrii Butenko in Bratislava. text:
GTA: San Andreas? Dang, you’re a baby!

We’re the original, baby! 

We played Atari 2600. Read to the end to find out which games! It was 1983 when we got that. 

At the same time we had some games on one of the first home computers ever offered for sale to the public, the Commodore 64. The “64” stands for 64 K, as in 64,000 bytes. But that sucked, cause you had to put in the floppy and then type a load command in a system similar to DOS, it was something like Load”Games”$$. I can’t remember it exactly but it had quotes and dollar signs and numbers. You didn’t just insert the game cartridge and hit the in button.

Maybe a computer geek on here can remember the loading commands and refresh my memory! Ha! 

Yep, wow! We’re ancient now. All of my childhood heros and stars are now elderly or dead. It’s kinda sad watching your childhood die, and knowing time will fly until we’re there too.

Those were the days. Back to games.
After the 64 they launched the 128, with you guessed it, a whopping 128,000 bytes of processing power. I think that’s where the tech rule of evolution began, the rule in which technology doubles in speed and processing power about every year. But things still looked kinda old world. Tech pieces were like furniture, like how TV’s and VCR’s even came in a real hardwood body/case. 

Yeah, Commodore’s sucked for games. But it was the beginning of an entire new world and a necessary step. My dad was an audiophile and tech junky, he even had one of the very first Sony VHS camcorders. 

The camera itself was the size of a bazooka, and the VHS tape went in a unit almost the size of a briefcase. If I am remembering correctly there was a second briefcase sized unit that was just the battery pack. All of it was connected by huge thick cords. I was really the first generation of kids that had a parent videoing us all the time, that wasn’t like the old film cameras needing developing. You could video something on a VHS tape, pop it out and put it in your VCR and instantly rewatch it. Haha!

Those were the days.

In elementary school we played the first games, the best games. We played Space Invaders, Pitfall and Frogger. Those were the original games, those were the best games.

The 80’s were the very best time to grow up. The moral and physical decay of America hadn’t really begun yet. 

It was a simple time in America. All the racism stuff from the civil rights movement era were over cause we had won the victory… and passed, and it had not yet been cooked back up by the elites, intentionally meant to divide and conquer the people. Reagan was president and the economy was BOOMING. 

We grew up watching the Cosby Show, Michael Jackson, Richard Prior, Eddie Murphy. Mike Tyson and Michael Jordan to name a few. Yes, some of them were secretly dirtbags. But it was an amazing time, black stars were the best and biggest in everything. I didn’t even know what racism was where I grew up. Jordan’s legendary soaring dunk with his tongue sticking out was posted on my wall right next to Tom Cruise in Top Gun, they were the kings of sports and media. They were the biggest stars.

The early to mid 80’s really were the best time to grow up. We didn’t yet know how evil and corrupt our own government was, and how FUBAR some of our stars were.

It was a simple time alright.
The 80’s was PEAK AMERICA!!!

(Apologies for the novel).

The Justice Department is investigating whether Nvidia tried to evade antitrust review in its deal with AI chip maker Groq. Groq called it a non exclusive licensing agreement letting Nvidia use its AI chips, with Groq's CEO and COO joining Nvidia.

AI firms have struck similar deals to license tech and hire top talent without outright acquisitions, often bypassing automatic government review meant to assess harm to competition.

Officials are weighing stricter scrutiny as they confront how few companies concentrate AI power. Sources say the probe began soon after the December announcement, with a formal information request to Nvidia. If wrongdoing is found, fines are possible but unwinding the deal is unlikely.

Nvidia says the Groq story shows the US system working as designed. The FTC is also reviewing such deals, and Senators Warren and Blumenthal have urged investigations, calling the arrangements mergers in effect that consolidate talent and resources while skirting review.

Right now, everyone is watching:

🛢️ Oil > $100

But there’s another force quietly putting pressure on U.S. stocks:

10Y Treasury Yield ≈ 4.84%

That puts it near its highest levels since November 2023.

Why does the 10Y matter so much?

Because it’s one of the most important anchors in the entire asset-pricing system.

Think about it simply:

If a risk-free Treasury can offer a yield close to 5%, why should investors pay extremely high P/E multiples today for profits that may not arrive until years from now?

The chain is straightforward:

10Y ↑

↓

Discount Rate ↑

↓

Present Value of Future Earnings ↓

↓

Growth Stock Valuations ↓

That’s why a high-yield environment tends to hit these areas hardest:

🔻 High-PE Tech
🔻 Software / SaaS
🔻 Small-Cap Growth
🔻 Unprofitable Growth
🔻 Highly Leveraged Companies
On the other hand, companies with:
Strong Cash Flow + Current Earnings + Pricing Power
become increasingly attractive.
And that’s the shift I see happening in the U.S. market right now.

Previously, investors were willing to pay for:

Growth at Any Price.

Now, the market is increasingly demanding:

Growth + Earnings + Cash Flow + Valuation

So there’s one number I’ll be watching very closely from here:

🔥 5%

If the 10Y continues moving toward 5%, we could see another round of valuation compression across the market.

Oil is the first hand applying pressure.

The 10Y Treasury may be the second hand squeezing valuations.

Watch the Yield. 👀

text:
look like markets trying to price in bull case scenario today. 

I was never excited by Apollo Finvest’s old “AWS of lending” story. It provided back-end tech and capital to digital-lending partners who owned the actual customer relationship. I saw no obvious reason why that setup alone would produce exceptional economics.
But their new D2C pivot, Apollo Cash, is a completely different animal.

Apollo now owns the app, the underwriting decision, and the collection cycle. If this model works, it could transform a tiny ₹153-crore micro-cap business. If it fails, the direct credit losses sit entirely with Apollo shareholders. That makes this shift much more interesting—and much more dangerous.
The early operational signs are definitely encouraging:
The Momentum: Monthly disbursements skyrocketed from just ₹30 lakh in February to ₹10.31 crore in July 2026.

The Scale: Over 1 lakh loans have been disbursed across 19,000 pin codes.
The Ticket Size: Average micro-loans sit around ₹3,750, targeting an underserved niche that traditional banks cannot process profitably due to heavy structural costs.
But there is a classic trap in digital lending. Demand is the easiest thing to demonstrate. When you offer immediate money to cash-starved customers, applications arrive like "water in a desert." The hard part isn't finding borrowers; it’s separating a good borrower facing a temporary cash crunch from a bad borrower who cannot or will not repay.

Management notes that most loans are now going to repeat users. This sounds brilliant on paper—small first loans establish trust, and repeat loans recover initial customer acquisition costs.

But do not fall for the cohort survival trap. If 100 people take a first loan and only 40 reach loan number four, assessing those surviving 40 in isolation makes the model look magnificent. But the defaults, collection costs, and ghosted accounts of the other 60 still mathematically belong to the economics of the original 100.

At ₹502, the market is pricing in a highly optimistic Bull Case. For an 18% return hurdle, Apollo Cash must prove that its repeat loans turn into durable, mature profitability after absorbing defaults and collection bills as the book expands.
Fast downloads alone do not build a moat. Watch the cohorts, not just the loan milestones.
Read the full deep-dive scenario modeling (Bear vs. Cautious Base vs. Bull Case) on my Substack. 👇

text:
NAIVE STROKES: ON THE COMMERCIALIZATION OF MATHEMATICS—

[summary]
AI changed knowledge work by introducing winner-take-all effects, increased competition against humans by AIs and the substitution of capital for labor. This is causing the "commercialization of mathematics" and the erosion of pre-existing professional norms. We should think about which other domains will be disrupted in the same way: entrance of millions more agents, elimination of inefficiencies, and accompanying replacement of professional etiquette for capitalistic ruthlessness.

[background]
On September 8th, 2026, OpenAI announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, a longstanding unsolved member of the seven Millennium Prize Problems posed six and one score years ago. OpenAI's solution was generated chiefly by an artificial intelligence system. Heated contention has erupted between career mathematicians on one side and OpenAI on the other on questions about credit assignment and spying. Somehow, the ivory tower of mathematics has become the playing ground of trillion-dollar tech companies. The commercialization of mathematics, once unthinkable, portends a kind of ruthless competition driven by AI that will breach all fields of human activity and quash professional norms of gentlemanly etiquette.

Essentially, OpenAI is accused of deliberately scooping another mathematician, Tristan Buckmaster, a maths professor at New York University. Buckmaster had been collaborating with Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, on solving Navier Stokes using AIs from OpenAI and Anthropic. Having caught wind of impending results from their effort to solve Navier Stokes, says Buckmaster, OpenAI then spent millions of dollars in compute to achieve a result first. Buckmaster says OpenAI has been dodgy about whether his personal data from conversations with ChatGPT were used in OpenAI's discovery. Furthermore, Buckmaster says he was offered authorship on OpenAI's discovery, but contingent on acknowledging that an internal OpenAI model resolved it, and also contingent on precluding Alpöge from authorship. Finally, Buckmaster suggests that senior OpenAI staffer Sebastien Bubeck threatened his career if he did not comply.

Such are the allegations. Particularly explosive is the claim that OpenAI somehow breached private user data to obtain an advantage in solving Navier-Stokes, with Buckmaster asking point-blank, "Is it ethical to use customer's data to try to scoop their customer?" In a written statement, he emphasizes that OpenAI's published approach is a "bright red flag" regarding spying because is "not the direction one arrives at in a few days by giving a model the problem statement" and happens to be the same strategy that he and Alpöge had "quietly chosen to attack". OpenAI has issued a careful denial, maintaining that neither human researchers nor AI agents involved from their side accessed "specific user data [...] in order to solve this problem", while also disclaiming that "we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models".

In the past 48 hours since the Navier Stokes announcement, additional suspicions of improper data use have been levied by other mathematicians towards OpenAI. Andreas Thom, a mathematician at TU Dresden, says that another recent mathematical scoop by OpenAI, that of the finding of a non-sofic group, also curiously resembles the methods and technique he used, which he also discussed with OpenAI's AI model ChatGPT. He says he also asked Bubeck and another OpenAI staffer whether his discussions with ChatGPT on finding a non-sofic group were somehow used for OpenAI's finding, only to receive a "unjustifiably broad and materially misleading" answer which was "plainly dishonest".

It would be a serious violation if OpenAI repeatedly leveraged private ChatGPT conversations to beat out multiple mathematicians to major discoveries. (No concrete records of this type of breach have been provided by the mathematicians.) Equally troubling is the nonchalant that's-how-it-goes stance adopted by OpenAI in its defence of scooping Alpöge and Buckmaster. The all's-fair-in-love-and-business attitude exhibited by OpenAI corporate boosters on X is the kind of defiant victor's justice customary to, say, two Silicon Valley companies racing to launch rival smartphones, or competing scooter apps. It is markedly not the kind of professional respect with which working mathematicians accord one another.

But that's precisely the point. Mathematics, once an exuberantly collaborative field which turned its nose down at the comparative viciousness of biology, medicine, or economics, has become a battlefield for AI companies. The PR bonanza of developing a model which can solve hard maths problems others cannot is evidently worth demolishing professional norms.

[body]
Now to the meat of the matter, which isn't the controversy proper. Gentlemanly norms such as those in mathematics - to wit, the implicit agreement not to scoop peers, the general openness with which to conduct affairs, the humility not to bag the limelight - are sustainable only in circumstances where everybody knows each other - so that friendliness is owed - where problems are very difficult - so that mutual assistance is desirable and neccessary - and where winning is not the end goal - the prizes are not claimed only by the winner, the prizes are not winner-take-all, and partial or incomplete discovery is still worth something.

These preconditions are all blown up, obviously, by AI, that is, by the competitive pressures induced by AI and by existence of AI agents themselves.

(Aside: Yes yes Newton-Leibniz; Perelman precedent yes yes. Exception proves the rule, mon frère. But actually, was it not the case that at least one if not more of the three preconditions from above did not hold in each of these circumstances? Moreover, no idiosyncratic man stands alone against a swarm.)

OpenAI's own statements about the matter already assume a competitive dynamic which Buckmaster probably didn't realize he was operating in. E.g. Sam: "We felt it was challenging to offer [paper authorship] to Levent (an Anthropic employee...)" or Sebastien: "[...] I felt it would be inappropriate for an Anthropic employee to author OpenAI’s work. Importantly it was admitted that internal Anthropic models had been used in their proof of Euler blowup; I therefore felt I could not consider Levent to be an independent academic. [...] I did not know how to navigate giving access to internal OpenAI IP to an Anthropic employee."

Sort of Buckmaster's fault, really. He should have known that his heroic two-man three-agent endeavour to solve Navier Stokes would never hold up to ten thousand machines operating in the trillion dollar IPO environment.

In the context of omg-mega-valuable-pretraining-secret of course it doesn't make sense to offer "internal IP" to a rival AI lab employee. In the context of mathematics, or most sciences, it's like, what do you mean, internal IP? But AI having mathematics under its Sauron's Eye of course makes everything more like the former. Why? Well obviously because the ability to solve these hardo problems depends on mega-valuable-training-secret. But also because the audience for such-and-such discovery is no longer other mathematicians, it's the stock market, which is definitely not composed of career mathematicians capable of understanding the nuance of contributed what when and is more about - well do you have the best model or no?

That's the inevitable consequence of the intelligence machine: it's all a capital game now, baby, more money more tokens more theorems.

Speaking from a personal perspective, what's unfolding in mathematics now is totally deja-vu-all-over-again from what I saw in machine learning (ML), which is what we used to call the field of AI before there was so much money in it. Back in the late 2010s when I started in ML, there was this shiny new thing, deep learning, and with it came a new way of doing science, which was like, publishing in conferences over publishing in journals, a huge focus on paper count, etc. Paper count was a big thing that oldheads would complain about. "Back in my day you could make professor with just two good journal papers and now even undergrads need five conference papers" etc etc. But like yeah that's what happens when (1) much faster progress is possible (2) there are a lot more participants (3) the rewards are much higher to winning. Up to this point in mathematics you simply couldn't make progress that quickly! That's why Navier Stokes took so long to solve (yes it's not fully solved etc). But with AI you can spin up literally 10k agents to do the equivalent of like, a century's worth of mathematics in a week, so you can solve stuff quickly. So then scooping is a thing.

That's part of the point I'm trying to make here, that the gentlemanly world of deep learning never came back, it will evaporate for mathematics and never come back, and it will also disappear and never come back for all the other domains. In ML, all the good work used to be done in academia, then as compute became more important, it was done at Google Brain and DeepMind and OpenAI, but at least everybody published, but then the papers were too valuable to publish because they were finally useful i.e. commercially valuable, so then they slowed publishing, but at least people still talked about stuff with each other and compared notes, but then ChatGPT came out, and now it's basically state secrets.

Monkey Paw Curls: if you asked most roboticists or NLP researchers in 2000s or 2010s of course they would be like, yes we would love to solve robotics or language, and make useful things for people (not all the scientists of course), but making useful things means giving up all the science and R&D to the companies.

Again, invention of the intelligence machine means you can throw money at a problem and get more intelligent person-hours on it which you could not before. So progress can be faster. More things are tractable. Also things are useful now. Toodle-doo, old norms of openness and collaboration.

I really want to emphasize that it is not simply the competitive dynamics of AI companies that induces competitive dynamics everywhere but also the mere existence of AI agents will inject competition everywhere because, well, you have more agents competing! Or from another POV we will improve market efficiencies everywhere. It's like, back in the day, you could find really lovely deals at the thrift store, so I'm told, but more market participants + better information flow = fewer good deals since everything is priced properly.

What else do we think is going to get swallowed by multi-agent swarms like this? Obviously Instinct et. al will destroy any kind of first-come-first-serve (FCFS) reservation system for restaurants by automating it. Online sneaker sales, btw, have long been botted to the nine circles of hell and back. Concert tickets too. For those two things the like Neanderthal equivalent of AGI, i.e. booking scripts / bots, is enough to unleash bidding wars. What's the implication or analogy? FCFS as an allocation mechanism is bidding through time (waiting) or effort (going in person etc) but agents are infinitely patient and workaholics so you can't use scarcity there anymore. So everything is price-based, lottery-based, or relationship-based atp. It's like not even clear to me that the latter two are better than price-based lwk.

Now at some point somebody will protest in the comments, "This all sucks and I'd like to return to the old way of things". Sure and do you go to the bowling alley? Insofar as adding friction would reinstate the Mesozoic here, I sure don't see anybody voting for sending Chicxulub back to space. Moloch wins again, is what a marsupial or Rat would say.

I will return to my old saw, hammering away that AGI Is Not Role Substitution. Astra is not replacing a single mathematician. It's more like, The Astra-Based-Swarm is Ending All of Mathematics.

Am I saying, w.r.t. Buckmaster Controversy etc, don't hate the player hate the game? Sort of, but not really? More like, there is only one game now, and it's the intelligence game? Nothing else matters on the hot path of RSI besides the hot path of RSI? Something like that. Goodbye Cenozoic Hello Noözoic.

text:
🇮🇳 Russia is pushing hard for a Su-57 deal ahead of Putin's visit, and India still isn't buying it.

Moscow's latest offer is generous. Full tech transfer, local manufacturing at HAL, even the newer twin-seat Su-57D, which completed its first test flight back in May.

Russian technicians actually visited HAL's Nasik facility last year, finding around 50 percent overlap with the existing Su-30MKI line.

India isn't impressed. Its own memory of the Su-57 goes back to the failed FGFA program, scrapped in 2018 after $295 million spent.

Back then, stealth on the sides and rear was weak, engines fell short of what was promised, and Russia refused to share source code.

India's focus has shifted firmly inward since. The Tejas Mk1A, Tejas Mk2, AMCA, and a major Su-30MKI upgrade now hold the real priority.

There's also a bigger risk hanging over this. Buying Su-57 could trigger CAATSA sanctions, right as India finalises a major trade deal aimed at cutting US tariffs to 18 percent.

The IAF currently runs just 29-31 squadrons against a sanctioned 42, and could lose up to 12 more by 2035 as older jets retire. Russia is betting that gap eventually forces India's hand.

I’m starting to watch something else:

How they are paying for it.

Amazon just raised £4.25 billion — about $5.76 billion — in its first-ever sterling bond sale.

Investor demand topped £10.65 billion.

Strong?

Yes.

Unlimited?

No.

Because the bigger number is this:

Hyperscalers have already issued more than $200 billion of debt in 2026.

That is more than double the total for all of 2025.

The AI boom is no longer just a semiconductor story.

It is becoming a capital-markets story.

The chain now looks like this:

AI models
→ GPUs
→ Data centers
→ Power infrastructure
→ Networking
→ Cooling
→ Debt issuance
And every step requires more capital.
What caught my attention is that Amazon’s new bond deal was covered roughly 2.5x.
Earlier this year, Alphabet’s sterling bond sale attracted demand of around 5x the amount offered.
That does not mean funding has dried up.
Far from it.
Amazon still raised nearly $6 billion.

But it does suggest something important:

Investor demand for hyperscaler debt is not infinite.

That matters because AI CapEx is moving from extraordinary to structural.

AMZN, GOOGL, MSFT and META are no longer funding a short investment cycle.

They are building infrastructure that may require years of sustained spending.

And that creates a new question for investors.

The first phase of the AI trade asked:

Who is willing to spend the most?

The next phase may ask:

Who can finance that spending at the lowest cost?

Because once borrowing costs rise, the economics change.

Higher yields
→ Higher financing costs
→ Higher hurdle rates
→ More pressure on AI project returns

The ECB has already warned that heavy hyperscaler borrowing could crowd out other issuers and push financing costs higher.

At the same time, lenders are becoming more selective across the broader AI-infrastructure market.

I’m watching:

→ AMZN
→ GOOGL
→ MSFT
→ META

My view:

The AI boom is not running out of money.
But money is starting to have a price again.
That distinction matters.
In the first phase, investors rewarded companies for spending aggressively on AI.

In the next phase, they may start asking whether every dollar of AI CapEx earns enough to justify the cost of the capital behind it.

AI infrastructure still needs GPUs.

It still needs power.

It still needs data centers.
But increasingly, it also needs something less exciting — and just as important:
Cheap financing.
The next bottleneck in AI may not be chips.

It may be capital.

text:
𝗧𝗵𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗱𝗮𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝘄𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘆-𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗱 𝗪𝗲𝗲𝗸 𝗶𝗻 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝗧𝗶𝗺𝗲 — 𝗦𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿 𝟭𝟬, 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲

1 Corinthians 8:1b-7, 11-13
Psalm 139:1b-3, 13-14ab, 23-24
Luke 6:27-38

𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘂𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗬𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗱𝗮𝘆

Paul has been teaching Christians how to live faithfully inside a pagan society. Today the issue becomes very practical. Some Corinthians know that pagan gods are false and therefore think they may freely eat meat associated with pagan sacrifices. They are correct about the idols, but Paul asks a deeper question: 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗮 𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗼𝗺 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗵𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗳𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝗶𝗻?

The Gospel takes the same principle much further. Paul says, “Be willing to surrender something lawful for your brother.” Jesus says, “Be willing even to love the man who hates you.”

The thread joining everything together is 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆: learning to value another person’s good more than our pride, possessions, retaliation, or insistence upon our rights.

𝗙𝗜𝗥𝗦𝗧 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗚
𝟭 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝟴:𝟭𝗯-𝟳, 𝟭𝟭-𝟭𝟯
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴?

Picture Corinth filled with pagan temples. Animals are sacrificed to false gods, portions are eaten in religious banquets, and sacrificial meat can enter ordinary social life.

Now picture two converts.

One knows perfectly well that Apollo is not a god. To him, the meat is simply meat.

The other spent perhaps twenty or thirty years worshiping those gods. He is now a Christian, but eating sacrificial meat still feels to him like returning to idolatry.

The first man says, “I know better.”

Paul replies, in effect:

𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗱. 𝗡𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗹𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿?

That is the problem behind the entire reading.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟭

“Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that ‘all of us possess knowledge.’ ‘Knowledge’ puffs up, but love builds up.”

The knowledgeable Corinthians are not wrong because they possess knowledge. Truth is good. Their danger is pride.

Imagine one saying, “Why should I change what I do because this other Christian doesn't understand theology as well as I do?”

That attitude reveals the problem. He knows something true about idols but has not yet understood what Christian knowledge is 𝗳𝗼𝗿.

Truth should lead us toward God and the good of our neighbor. When knowledge instead becomes a reason to look down upon another person, it has become spiritually disordered.

𝗕𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝗼𝗹𝘆.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟮

“If any one imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.”

Paul is not praising ignorance.

He is attacking conceit.

A person can possess the correct answer and still misunderstand how that truth should govern his conduct.

The Corinthian says:

“I know idols are nothing.”

Paul says:

“Then you should also know that your brother's soul matters more than proving that you are right.”

Knowledge reaches its proper perfection when it is governed by wisdom and charity.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟯

“But if one loves God, one is known by him.”

Paul turns the man's attention away from himself.

The boast was:

“Look what 𝗜 know.”

Paul redirects him:

“What matters is belonging to God and loving Him.”

And love of God cannot be separated from love of the person who belongs to God.

Paul is already preparing the devastating description he will use later:

𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗲𝗮𝗸 𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝘀 “𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘄𝗵𝗼𝗺 𝗖𝗵𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗲𝗱.”

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟰

“Hence, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that ‘an idol has no real existence,’ and that ‘there is no God but one.’”

Now Paul says plainly that the knowledgeable Christian's theology is correct.

The statue exists.

The supposed god represented by it does not.

Apollo is not a competing deity whom Christians must fear.

Therefore the meat has not acquired some magical divine quality merely because pagans offered it before an idol.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀. There is one God.

But Paul does not conclude, “Therefore do whatever you want.”

That is exactly where the Corinthians are going wrong.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟱

“For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many ‘gods’ and many ‘lords’—”

Walk through Corinth and you would encounter temples, statues, religious festivals, household gods, stories of divine beings, and rulers claiming exalted titles.

Paul acknowledges that the world is full of beings 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗱 gods.

He does not concede that they really are gods.

The distinction is important. Christianity does not claim that our God happens to be stronger than Apollo.

It claims that Apollo 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗚𝗼𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗹𝗹.

There is an infinite distinction between Creator and creature.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟲

“yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.”

Paul now places Jesus within the identity and creative work of the one God.

Everything is from the Father and everything is through the Son.

Christ therefore cannot simply be one more creature among the “many lords.” Creatures exist 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 Him.

So Paul is not weakening monotheism. He is revealing its Christian depth.

The Father is God. The Son is Lord. They are personally distinct while belonging to the one divine reality.

And this matters to Paul's argument because the Christian's entire existence is now ordered to God.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟳

“However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through being hitherto accustomed to idols, eat food as really offered to an idol; and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.”

Here is the man Paul has been concerned about.

Imagine that six months ago this Christian was still worshiping in Apollo's temple.

He sacrificed there.

He prayed there.

He ate ritual meals there.

Now he has been baptized and believes in Christ.

He intellectually hears, “Apollo is nothing.”

But years of association do not disappear overnight.

Then he sees a mature Christian eating the sacrificial meat.

He thinks:

“Well, he is doing it. Maybe I should do it too.”

But inside his conscience is saying:

“𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀.”

He eats anyway.

Now we can finally see Paul's concern.

The meat itself is not the central problem.

The weaker man has just practiced doing something while believing that he is offending God.

He is training himself to disregard conscience.

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿.

His conscience needs to be 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗱 so that eventually he understands the truth. But until then, the stronger Christian should not push him into acting against it.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝟴-𝟭𝟬?

Today's reading skips these verses, but they explain the transition.

Paul says food itself does not bring us nearer to God. Then he warns that the stronger Christian's “liberty” can become a stumbling block.

He even imagines the weaker believer seeing the knowledgeable Christian eating in an idol's temple and being emboldened to imitate him.

Now verse 11 lands with its full force.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟭𝟭

“And so by your knowledge this weak man is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died.”

Paul deliberately changes the way the stronger Christian looks at this man.

Previously he may have thought:

“That ignorant fellow.”

Paul says:

No.

𝗛𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿.

And more than that:

𝗖𝗵𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗵𝗶𝗺.

Now put the two things on a scale.

On one side:

“My right to eat this meat.”

On the other:

“The spiritual welfare of a man for whom Jesus shed His blood.”

Suddenly the argument becomes almost embarrassingly simple.

𝗖𝗵𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝗴𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗛𝗶𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗳𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗵𝗶𝗺. 𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘂𝗽 𝗮 𝗽𝗶𝗲𝗰𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝘁?

Notice also the seriousness of “destroyed.” Paul does not treat the Christian life as though another believer's perseverance were irrelevant because his salvation were automatically guaranteed regardless of what happens. The possibility of genuine spiritual ruin is precisely why scandal is so serious.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟭𝟮

“Thus, sinning against your brethren and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.”

Now Paul says something astonishing.

When you spiritually wound your brother, 𝗖𝗵𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝘁 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆.

Why?

Because the Christian is joined to Christ.

Christianity does not create millions of isolated relationships with Jesus. Baptism joins believers to Christ and therefore to one another.

So scandal is not merely:

“I offended somebody.”

Biblical scandal means that my conduct becomes an occasion for another person's spiritual fall.

That is why Paul calls it sin against Christ Himself.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟭𝟯

“Therefore, if food is a cause of my brother’s falling, I will never eat meat, lest I cause my brother to fall.”

Now Paul's conclusion is perfectly clear.

He does 𝗻𝗼𝘁 suddenly decide that meat is evil.

He decides that his brother is more valuable than meat.

This is Christian freedom at its highest.

The immature man says:

“I'm free, therefore nobody can stop me.”

The mature Christian says:

“I'm so free that I can willingly surrender something lawful when love requires it.”

𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗼𝘆 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗼𝗺. 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗼𝗺 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿.

𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗣𝗢𝗡𝗦𝗢𝗥𝗜𝗔𝗟 𝗣𝗦𝗔𝗟𝗠
𝗣𝘀𝗮𝗹𝗺 𝟭𝟯𝟵:𝟭𝗯-𝟯, 𝟭𝟯-𝟭𝟰𝗮𝗯, 𝟮𝟯-𝟮𝟰

“Thou knowest when I sit down and when I rise up; thou discernest my thoughts from afar. Thou searchest out my path and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways.

For thou didst form my inward parts, thou didst knit me together in my mother’s womb. I praise thee, for thou art fearful and wonderful. Wonderful are thy works!

Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!”

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝘀𝗮𝗹𝗺 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲?

Immediately after Paul has exposed the possibility of self-deception, the Church gives us this Psalm.

The Corinthian could say:

“I know I'm right.”

The Psalmist says:

“𝗚𝗼𝗱, 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝗲.”

That is much more searching.

God sees not only what we do but why we do it. He sees whether “defending truth” is secretly pride. He sees whether “exercising freedom” is actually selfishness. He sees whether our insistence upon being right is costing someone else spiritually.

And the Psalm does not end:

“God, tell me how right I am.”

It ends:

𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝗲.

That is genuine humility.

The man who wants holiness does not merely examine everybody else's errors. He opens his own heart before God and asks Him to reveal whatever is crooked.

𝗚𝗢𝗦𝗣𝗘𝗟
𝗟𝘂𝗸𝗲 𝟲:𝟮𝟳-𝟯𝟴
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴?

Jesus is speaking directly to His disciples.

Now imagine the people He describes.

Someone hates you.

Someone curses you.

Someone abuses you.

Someone strikes you.

Someone takes what belongs to you.

Jesus is not talking about theoretical niceness.

He is asking:

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗮 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗯𝗼𝗱𝘆 𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗶𝗺 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗼𝘃𝗲?

Our instinct is reciprocity:

“You're good to me, so I'll be good to you.”

“You hurt me, so I'll hurt you.”

Jesus is about to replace that entire system with imitation of the Father.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝟮𝟳-𝟮𝟴

“But I say to you that hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.”

Do not imagine merely an annoying person.

Think of someone who actually hates you.

Jesus does not merely command:

“Don't kill him.”

He gives four movements:

Love him.

Do good to him.

Bless him.

Pray for him.

That immediately tells us that Christian love is not identical with pleasant emotion.

Jesus cannot command you suddenly to feel warm affection.

He commands the will.

You can sincerely say:

“I dislike what this man has done. I may feel deeply wounded. But I will not desire his damnation or evil. I will his true good before God.”

You can pray:

“Lord, convert him. Forgive him. Make him holy. Save his soul.”

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗹𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗲𝘀.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝟮𝟵-𝟯𝟬

“To him who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also; and from him who takes away your cloak do not withhold your coat as well. Give to every one who begs from you; and of him who takes away your goods do not ask them again.”

Jesus is attacking the instinct of retaliation.

Someone humiliates you.

Immediately something inside says:

“Now I get even.”

Jesus teaches His disciple not to become morally controlled by the sinner.

The command does not mean that justice ceases to matter or that we must allow innocent people to be abused without protection.

It means something deeper:

𝗔𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗮𝗻'𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗻 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗵𝗶𝗺 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗜 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲.

If he hates, I need not become hateful.

If he curses, I need not curse.

If he is merciless, I remain called to mercy.

That is spiritual freedom.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟯𝟭

“And as you wish that men would do to you, do so to them.”

This is much stronger than simply saying:

“Don't harm people.”

Jesus commands positive charity.

Ask yourself:

“If I were frightened, weak, confused, poor, sinful, lonely, or struggling, how would I hope another Christian would treat me?”

Then treat him that way.

The Golden Rule therefore requires imagination. I must step outside myself long enough to see another person's needs from his position.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝟯𝟮-𝟯𝟰

“If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.

And if you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same.

And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to receive as much again.”

Jesus now exposes ordinary human goodness.

Suppose I love my family because my family loves me.

Good.

But pagans do that.

Suppose I help the man who will later help me.

Again, even sinners understand reciprocal benefit.

Jesus therefore asks the uncomfortable question:

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗹𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝗚𝗼𝗱'𝘀 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗲?

If I love only those who reward me, Christianity has not yet transformed much.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟯𝟱

“But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return; and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High; for he is kind to the ungrateful and the selfish.”

Now Jesus reveals the reason.

Why love enemies?

Because 𝗚𝗼𝗱 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀.

God gives life, food, rain, opportunities for repentance, earthly blessings, and countless gifts even to people who reject Him.

Therefore the disciple is to resemble his Father.

This is what grace does.

Grace does not simply leave us exactly as we were while changing an entry in heaven's bookkeeping.

Grace heals and elevates the person so that the child begins increasingly to resemble his Father.

And Jesus even speaks explicitly of reward.

The Catholic understanding has no difficulty holding grace, transformed obedience, and reward together. God gives the grace by which His children act, and He freely crowns those grace-enabled acts.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟯𝟲

“Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.”

Here is the center of the Gospel.

Jesus does not say merely:

“Follow these rules.”

He says:

𝗟𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗙𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿.

Why forgive?

Because your Father is merciful.

Why love enemies?

Because your Father is merciful.

Why refuse vengeance?

Because your Father is merciful.

Why give generously?

Because your Father is merciful.

Christian morality is therefore ultimately participation in God's own goodness.

Holiness means becoming, by grace, what God's adopted children ought to resemble.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟯𝟳

“Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven.”

This verse does 𝗻𝗼𝘁 mean:

“Never say an action is sinful.”

Jesus Himself identifies sin and commands repentance.

The Church must discern good from evil.

The prohibition concerns the proud and condemnatory judgment by which I act as though I possess God's knowledge of another person's heart and final destiny.

I may rightly say:

“That action is objectively sinful.”

I cannot simply presume:

“I know everything in this man's heart, the degree of his guilt, and where God will finally judge his soul.”

Then Jesus adds forgiveness.

Why?

Because a man living entirely from God's mercy cannot consistently demand mercy for himself while refusing it to everyone else.

𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝟯𝟴

“give, and it will be given to you; good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For the measure you give will be the measure you get back.”

Picture someone buying grain.

The seller fills the container.

Then presses the grain down.

Shakes it so the empty spaces disappear.

Adds more.

Then fills it until it runs over.

Jesus uses that familiar picture to describe divine generosity.

God is not miserly.

But Jesus immediately attaches a warning:

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝘁𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂.

That should destroy complacency.

The Christian cannot say:

“God must forgive me endlessly, but I will remain merciless toward everyone who hurts me.”

Jesus connects the mercy we have received with the mercy we must practice.

𝗖𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗟 𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗠𝗘 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗚𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗞𝗔𝗚𝗘

Now the readings fit together.

Paul begins with a piece of meat.

𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁.

But if eating it seriously endangers your brother, love says:

“Give it up.”

The Psalm then takes us inside ourselves:

𝗚𝗼𝗱, 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝘆 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘁.

Do not merely show me whether my argument is correct. Show me whether pride, selfishness, retaliation, or hardness is hiding beneath it.

Then Jesus takes Paul's principle to its supernatural summit.

Paul says:

𝗟𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗹𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀.

Jesus says:

𝗟𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗺𝘆 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗹𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘃𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲.

Both confront the same instinct:

“But I have the right!”

Sometimes you do.

But Christ teaches something greater than possessing rights.

𝗛𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀 𝘂𝘀 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝘂𝗽𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺.

𝗦𝗨𝗠𝗠𝗔𝗥𝗬 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗘𝗫𝗛𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡

Today's readings ask one question in progressively harder forms:

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗺 𝗜 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘂𝗽 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗹𝗼𝘃𝗲?

Paul says:

Give up the meat.

The Psalm says:

Give up the pride that assumes your heart needs no examination.

Jesus says:

Give up retaliation.

Give up hatred.

Give up the insistence upon repayment.

Give up the desire to condemn.

Give mercy.

Give forgiveness.

Give love even where love is not returned.

And Christ does not command something He Himself refused to do.

The brother Paul tells us to protect is 𝗮 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘄𝗵𝗼𝗺 𝗖𝗵𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗲𝗱.

At the Cross, Christ loved enemies, prayed for persecutors, forgave sinners, and surrendered far more than a piece of meat.

So today's examination of conscience becomes very concrete:

Is there something I keep defending by saying:

“𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝗜 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀”?

Is exercising that right helping another person toward God or making his road harder?

Is there someone whose hatred of me has begun determining how I treat him?

Is there someone I want God to punish more than I want God to convert?

Is there someone from whom I demand a mercy that I refuse to give?

Then today's readings give us one prayer:

𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝗲, 𝗢 𝗚𝗼𝗱.

And one command:

𝗕𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝗳𝘂𝗹, 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗮𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗙𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝗳𝘂𝗹.

And one great lesson:

𝗖𝗵𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗼𝗺 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗱𝗼 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝗮𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗚𝗼𝗱.

text:
Manoj Sinha, the Delhi-installed Lieutenant Governor who took charge of occupied Kashmir on 7 August 2020 is now walking the streets of Chicago. This is the same man who, as the visible face of Indian occupation in a land the United Nations has recognised as disputed, oversaw a campaign of barbaric force against a people who have never been allowed to decide their own political future.

For more than half a decade, he functioned as the enforcer of an illegal occupation. Under his watch, Indian military forces carried out killings, leaving bodies and broken families in their wake. The bodies of Kashmiri resistance fighters are snatched and buried without any proper Islamic burial rites, far away from their families. Even after their death, the dead remain under constant watch and no one is allowed to offer any prayers or pay obeisance at their graves. Houses are blown up in the name of operations while entire mohallas are made to watch their homes being turned to rubble. Land is grabbed and property transferred in ways that serve the occupier’s long-term design. Kashmiris are framed on trumped-up charges, thrown into prisons far from their homes and government employees are dismissed on fabricated charges. Their suspension orders are directly issued from the Lieutenant Governor’s office.

That this same official now moves freely through Chicago, addressing gatherings and speaking as if he were a respectable public figure, exposes the emptiness of the slogans that powerful states recite about rights, justice and a rules-based world. The United Nations, which still describes Kashmir as a disputed territory and whose resolutions on self-determination remain unimplemented, sits in the same country that has given Sinha unhindered passage. A man who spent years tightening the grip of occupation over a population denied its political choice is treated as a guest rather than as someone answerable for what was done in his name. 

This insult is sharper for those who live under that occupation. An occupier’s appointee leaves the Valley he helped crush ruthlessly and is received without consequence in a city that claims to stand for liberty. The fact that this war criminal can roam Chicago after years of repression only confirms how cheap the language of justice has become when the victim is a Kashmiri.
